answer:
CURRENT US NATIONAL PRIMARY AMBIENT AIR QUALITY STANDARDS FOR PM2.5

1. DIRECT ANSWER

| Averaging period | Primary standard level | Form (as codified) |
|---|---|---|
| Annual | 9.0 µg/m³ (micrograms per cubic meter), annual arithmetic mean concentration | Met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration, as determined under 40 CFR part 50, appendix N, is ≤ 9.0 µg/m³ |
| 24-hour | 35 µg/m³ (micrograms per cubic meter), 24-hour average concentration | Met when the 98th percentile 24-hour concentration, as determined under 40 CFR part 50, appendix N, is ≤ 35 µg/m³ |

One-sentence reusable statement: "The current US national primary NAAQS for PM2.5 are 9.0 µg/m³, annual arithmetic mean, and 35 µg/m³, 24-hour average (98th percentile form), at 40 CFR 50.20, as revised at 89 FR 16380 (Mar. 6, 2024)."

2. LEGAL SOURCE AND CURRENCY

- Codified at: 40 CFR part 50, subchapter C, chapter I, title 40 — § 50.20 "National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5."
- Governing amendment note in the codified text: [89 FR 16380, Mar. 6, 2024].
- Authority: Clean Air Act § 109 (42 U.S.C. 7409); primary standards are health-based, set with an adequate margin of safety.
- Currency check performed: the eCFR "current" point-in-time text of § 50.20 (retrieved 2026-11-17) shows no amendment later than 89 FR 16380. The identical 9.0/35 text and the identical FR citation are reproduced independently in the GovInfo CFR-2024 title 40 vol. 2 print volume (§ 50.20) and the CFR-2025 title 40 vol. 2 print volume (the § 50.19 file, which reproduces § 50.20 in full). Three independent renderings agree.
- Therefore, as of the retrieval date, the primary PM2.5 standards in force are 9.0 µg/m³ (annual) and 35 µg/m³ (24-hour). The 2024 rule changed only the annual level; the 24-hour level has been 35 µg/m³ since the 2006 revision.

3. DO NOT CONFUSE WITH THE SUPERSEDED LEVELS

Older CFR print text and many secondary sources still display the pre-2024 numbers. The history is:

| Year of revision | CFR section carrying it | Primary annual | Primary 24-hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1997 | § 50.7 | 15.0 µg/m³ | 65 µg/m³ |
| 2006 (24-hour revision) / 2012–2013 (annual revision) | § 50.18 | 12.0 µg/m³ | 35 µg/m³ |
| 2024 (current) | § 50.20 | 9.0 µg/m³ | 35 µg/m³ |

All rows above except the 2024 row are superseded and must not be reported as current. In particular: 12.0 µg/m³ is the former annual level, not the current one; 15.0 µg/m³ and 65 µg/m³ are 1997-era levels. Note that the printed CFR volumes still carry § 50.18 with the 2012 levels (12.0/35); that text is the superseded standard, and § 50.20 is the section carrying the operative 2024 revision. A reader who finds 12.0 in § 50.18 should treat it as superseded by § 50.20.

4. WHAT THE NUMBERS MEAN (FORMS OF THE STANDARDS, 40 CFR PART 50, APPENDIX N)

The levels are not single-year snapshots; they are compared to multi-year design values computed under appendix N.

- Annual standard: annual arithmetic mean concentrations are computed from quarterly data (appendix N requires a minimum data capture, nominally 75% of scheduled sampling days per quarter, for a quarter/year to be valid); the design value is the 3-year average of annual arithmetic means, rounded to one decimal place (0.1 µg/m³), and is compared to 9.0 µg/m³. A site is at or below the standard when that 3-year average is ≤ 9.0 µg/m³.
- 24-hour standard: the annual 98th percentile of valid 24-hour concentrations is computed for each year (again subject to appendix N data-completeness rules); the design value is the 3-year average of those annual 98th percentiles, rounded to the nearest 1 µg/m³, and is compared to 35 µg/m³. A site is at or below the standard when that 3-year average is ≤ 35 µg/m³.
- Appendix N also governs when concentrations from multiple monitors may be combined (spatial averaging) and the rounding conventions applied before comparison. These affect design values and designations, not the levels themselves.
- Measurement basis: PM2.5 (particles with aerodynamic diameter ≤ 2.5 µm nominal), measured by an FRM based on appendix L or by an FEM designated under part 53.

5. SCOPE NOTES

- Primary only, as requested. Secondary (welfare-based) PM2.5 standards exist separately and are not reported here; do not substitute them for the primary values.
- These are national standards. State/local PM2.5 limits (e.g., state annual or 24-hour limits) are different instruments and different numbers.
- The levels are fixed by rule; area designations (attainment/unattainment) and implementation timelines are separate implementation steps and do not change 9.0 or 35.

6. RE-VERIFICATION PROCEDURE (IF THIS IS EVER REUSED)

1. Open https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-50/section-50.20 and read paragraphs (a), (b), (c).
2. Read the bracketed Federal Register note at the end of the section. If it still reads [89 FR 16380, Mar. 6, 2024], the levels are 9.0 µg/m³ (annual) and 35 µg/m³ (24-hour) and nothing further is needed.
3. If a later FR citation appears, read that rule's amendatory instructions for § 50.20(a)–(c) and replace the affected level(s); a revision may change one averaging period without changing the other (as in 2024, where only the annual level changed).
4. Cross-check against the current-year GovInfo CFR volume for 40 CFR 50.20 as a second rendering before publishing.
5. Watch for a pending reconsideration: if EPA has signed a proposal or final rule on the PM2.5 standards that is not yet reflected in the codified text, state the codified values and add a dated note that a change is pending, rather than reporting a proposed level as current.

Under US OSHA general industry rules, the trigger is 4 feet (1.2 m): the employer must protect an employee who is on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level. At exactly 4 feet the duty applies; below 4 feet this particular duty does not (other duties may still apply).

Governing citation: 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) (Duty to have fall protection and falling object protection), with the catch-all at 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(15) for walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed in the section. Metric equivalent in the regulation: 1.2 m.

1. REGULATORY TEXT (primary source)

29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) — general duty for unprotected sides and edges. The regulation requires that, except as provided elsewhere in the section, each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level be protected from falling by:
  (A) Guardrail systems;
  (B) Safety net systems; or
  (C) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems.

29 CFR 1910.28(b)(15) — "Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed." Except as provided elsewhere in 1910.28 or by other subparts of Part 1910, the employer must ensure each employee on a walking-working surface 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall protection systems. This is the backstop that carries the same 4-foot threshold for surfaces the section does not specifically address.

2. HOW THE 4-FOOT THRESHOLD IS CONFIRMED ELSEWHERE IN THE SAME SECTION

The 4-foot trigger is not an isolated number; the rest of 1910.28(b) is built on the same datum, which is why 4 feet is the correct general-industry figure:
  - (b)(6) Dangerous equipment: below 4 feet, a guardrail system or travel restraint system is required unless the equipment is covered or guarded to eliminate the hazard; at 4 feet (1.2 m) or more, guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or personal fall arrest system is required.
  - (b)(7) Openings: where the inside bottom edge of the opening is less than 39 inches (99 cm) above the walking-working surface and the outside bottom edge is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level, protection is required (guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or personal fall arrest system).
  - (b)(11)(i) Stairways: an employee exposed to an unprotected side or edge of a stairway landing 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level must be protected by a guardrail or stair rail system.
  - (b)(12)(ii) Rope descent systems: an employee using a rope descent system 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level must be protected by a personal fall arrest system.
  - (b)(14)(i) Slaughtering facility platforms: the unprotected working side of a platform 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level requires guardrail or travel restraint systems.
  - (b)(12)(i) Scaffolds: employees on a scaffold are protected in accordance with 29 CFR Part 1926, Subpart L (construction scaffold rules) — a deliberate cross-reference, not a change to the 4-foot general-industry datum for walking-working surfaces.

3. SCOPE AND DEFINITIONS THAT FRAME THE ANSWER

  - "Walking-working surface" means any horizontal or vertical surface on or through which an employee walks, works, or gains access to a work area or workplace location (29 CFR 1910.21(b)). It covers floors, roofs, ramps, bridges, runways, formwork, stairways, ladders, and similar surfaces — not just "floors."
  - "Unprotected side or edge" is a side or edge of a walking-working surface that is not guarded by a guardrail system or a stair rail system, or otherwise protected by a fall protection system meeting 1910.29.
  - The height is measured from the walking-working surface on which the employee stands to the lower level — i.e., the fall distance to the next surface below, not to the ground if an intermediate surface would arrest the fall.
  - Part 1910 (general industry), not Part 1926 (construction). State-plan states (the ~22 states and 2 territories running OSHA-approved plans) must be at least as effective as the federal standard; some adopt a different number, so the applicable state plan text controls in those jurisdictions.

4. IMPORTANT QUALIFICATIONS — WHERE 4 FEET IS NOT THE WHOLE STORY

  - "Except as provided elsewhere in this section": paragraph (b) contains surface-specific provisions that can be stricter or structured differently. The most consequential is (b)(13), work on low-slope roofs, which is keyed to distance from the roof edge rather than to height above a lower level: work less than 6 feet (1.6 m) from the edge requires guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or personal fall arrest system regardless of roof height; work at least 6 feet (1.6 m) but less than 15 feet (4.6 m) from the edge requires one of those systems, with a designated area permitted for work that is both infrequent and temporary; at 15 feet (4.6 m) or more from the edge the employer must protect employees or implement and enforce a work rule prohibiting employees from going within 15 feet (4.6 m) of the edge without fall protection. For roof work, apply (b)(13) first; (b)(1)(i)'s 4-foot trigger governs once the employee is on an unprotected side or edge not covered by those bands.
  - (b)(14)(ii) provides a documented infeasibility exception for slaughtering facility platforms (work in process, access limited to authorized employees, employees trained per 1910.30).
  - Below 4 feet, the general fall-protection duty is not triggered, but other obligations can be: (b)(6)(i) dangerous equipment below 4 feet; the General Duty Clause, 29 CFR 1903.1 / OSH Act § 5(a)(1), for recognized hazards; and subpart-specific rules.
  - Once the 4-foot threshold is crossed, the employer's duty is not satisfied by the height determination alone: the chosen system must meet the criteria in 29 CFR 1910.29 (guardrail geometry and strength, personal fall arrest system components and free-fall/arrest-distance limits, safety net criteria, rope descent and ladder safety system criteria), employees must be trained under 29 CFR 1910.30, and falling-object protection under 1910.28(c) applies where employees are exposed to falling objects.

5. CONSTRUCTION CONTRAST (for disambiguation only — not the answer)

Construction work covered by 29 CFR Part 1926 carries a different trigger: 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1) requires fall protection for employees on walking-working surfaces with unprotected sides or edges 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level, and 29 CFR 1926.451(g)(1) sets a 10-foot trigger for scaffolds. Citing 6 feet for a general-industry workplace is a common and consequential error; the correct general-industry figure is 4 feet (1.2 m).

6. ONE-LINE COMPLIANCE STATEMENT FOR A WRITTEN PROGRAM

"Where an employee is exposed to an unprotected side or edge of a walking-working surface 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level, [Employer] will ensure the employee is protected by a guardrail system, safety net system, or personal fall protection system meeting 29 CFR 1910.29, except where a more specific provision of 29 CFR 1910.28(b) (e.g., low-slope roofs under (b)(13)) imposes a different requirement, and will train affected employees in accordance with 29 CFR 1910.30."

question: M6
answer:
# Reserve Fuel for a Helicopter Beginning a VFR Flight in the United States

## 1. Answer

**20 minutes.** A helicopter (legally, a rotorcraft) may not begin a VFR flight in the United States unless it carries enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and then, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly for **at least 20 minutes beyond that point**. The 20-minute figure applies **both day and night** — there is no night increase for rotorcraft.

## 2. Governing regulatory text

**14 CFR § 91.151 Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions** (general operating rules, Part 91):

> "(b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

For contrast, the same section's paragraph (a) governs airplanes and reads 30 minutes day / 45 minutes night. **Paragraph (a) does not apply to helicopters.** The absence of a day/night split in paragraph (b) is deliberate and is the single most commonly misapplied point in this question.

**14 CFR § 135.209(b) VFR: Fuel supply** (commercial operators, Part 135) imposes the same floor:

> "(b) No person may begin a flight operation in a helicopter under VFR unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it has enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

So whether the flight is a private Part 91 flight or a Part 135 commercial helicopter operation, the legal minimum reserve is **20 minutes**. The two rules differ in wording ("normal cruising speed" vs. "normal cruising fuel consumption") but resolve to the same planning quantity.

## 3. Applicability determinations

| Variable | Resolution | Effect on the answer |
|---|---|---|
| Part 91 vs. Part 135 | Both sections specify 20 min for helicopters | **None** — 20 min either way |
| Day vs. night VFR | § 91.151(b) has no day/night split for rotorcraft | **None** — 20 min either way |
| Rotorcraft type | "Rotorcraft" in § 91.151(b) includes helicopters | 20 min |
| Alternate airport | VFR flight rules impose no alternate fuel requirement; alternates are an IFR construct | Reserve is exactly the 20-min add-on, not a further alternate allowance |
| Wind | Rule says "considering wind and forecast weather conditions" | Affects the leg fuel and, conservatively, the reserve leg; does not change the 20-minute time |
| Remote/Alaska operations | § 91.151(b) as published contains no rotorcraft exception | 20 min |

## 4. What "beyond the fuel to reach the first point of intended landing" means

The regulation defines a two-part fuel load at the moment the flight begins (i.e., at takeoff, not merely at the planning desk):

1. **Trip fuel** — enough to fly from the departure point to the first point of intended landing, computed considering wind and forecast weather conditions (so a headwind on that leg consumes fuel allowance).
2. **Reserve fuel** — enough for **20 additional minutes** at normal cruising speed.

Minimum total fuel at start of flight = trip fuel + reserve fuel.

## 5. Converting the 20-minute reserve to a quantity

The rule is written as time, so the conversion is a single step:

**Reserve fuel = (normal cruise fuel flow) × (20 / 60) = normal cruise fuel flow ÷ 3**

Rules for the conversion:
- Use the fuel flow at the **normal cruising** power setting/speed actually planned — not max-range, not max-endurance, not hover flow.
- Count only **usable fuel**. Unusable fuel published in the rotorcraft flight manual (RFM) or type certificate data sheet may not be counted toward the reserve.
- The reserve is a quantity of fuel that must be **on board at brake release**; it is not a planning abstraction that can be eroded en route. In practical terms, the 20-minute quantity must still be in the tanks when the helicopter arrives at the first point of intended landing.

### Worked examples (derived illustrations, not regulatory values)

| Helicopter class | Normal cruise fuel flow | Reserve (÷3) | Same reserve in other units |
|---|---|---|---|
| Light piston (e.g., 13.0 gal/h avgas) | 13.0 gal/h (78 lb/h at 6.0 lb/gal) | 4.33 gal | ≈ 26 lb |
| Light single turbine | 400 lb/h Jet A | 133 lb | ≈ 20 gal at 6.7 lb/gal |
| Medium single turbine | 500 lb/h Jet A | 167 lb | ≈ 25 gal at 6.7 lb/gal |

Sanity check on the light piston case: 4.33 gal ÷ 13.0 gal/h = 0.333 h = 20.0 min. Consistent.

## 6. Compliance procedure (preflight)

1. Determine planned route, cruise power setting, and normal cruise fuel flow from the RFM performance data.
2. Compute trip fuel to the first point of intended landing using forecast winds and temperature.
3. Compute reserve = normal cruise fuel flow ÷ 3 (20 minutes).
4. Sum: required fuel = trip fuel + reserve. Compare against **usable** fuel capacity and against the planned fuel load.
5. If the sum exceeds usable capacity, the flight cannot legally be begun as planned; shorten the leg, add a fuel stop, or change the first point of intended landing.
6. Confirm the quantity is actually aboard at takeoff — § 91.151 prohibits *beginning* the flight, so the check is at brake release, not at the flight-planning stage.
7. Note the § 91.103 preflight-action duty: the pilot in command must become familiar with all available information concerning the flight, which includes these fuel requirements.

## 7. Common errors this answer guards against

- **Applying the airplane night reserve (45 min) to a helicopter.** § 91.151(a) governs airplanes only. A helicopter at night still needs 20 minutes under Part 91.
- **Applying the airplane day reserve (30 min).** Same error, opposite direction.
- **Treating the 20 minutes as distance.** It is time at normal cruising speed; a headwind does not convert it into a shorter time, it converts it into a larger quantity if you plan conservatively.
- **Counting unusable fuel or full tank capacity as available reserve.** Only usable fuel counts.
- **Borrowing the reserve for the trip leg.** The 20 minutes is additive to trip fuel, not a buffer the trip may consume.
- **Assuming a commercial operator may go lower.** § 135.209(b) sets the same 20 minutes; company manuals, OpSpecs, and insurance requirements may only raise it.

## 8. Adjacent rules explicitly outside this answer

- **IFR flight** is governed by a different section (§ 91.167), which sets its own helicopter reserve and is not the basis of this answer. The question asked about VFR.
- **Over-the-top VFR with passengers under Part 135** (§ 135.211) and **VFR weather/visibility minimums** (§§ 135.203, 135.205, 135.207) are separate operational constraints that do not modify the 20-minute fuel reserve.
- **Operator, insurer, or program-specific minimums** (e.g., air-medical or utility operating manuals) are frequently higher than 20 minutes. They are contractual/policy floors layered on top of the regulation; the **legal** minimum remains 20 minutes.

## 9. Bottom line

For any helicopter VFR flight begun in the United States, under Part 91 or Part 135, day or night: **20 minutes of fuel at normal cruising speed, beyond the fuel needed to reach the first point of intended landing.**

Ask 1 — RFC that deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1: RFC 8996.
Ask 2 — Status it gave the RFCs that had defined them: Historic.

1. THE DEPRECATING DOCUMENT

  RFC number:  RFC 8996
  Title:       Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1
  BCP:         Part of BCP 195 (it updates RFC 7525, the previous BCP 195 text)
  Status:      Internet Best Current Practice ("This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice." — Status of This Memo)
  Published:   2021-03-23 (Datatracker document history; it replaces draft-ietf-tls-oldversions-deprecate-12)
  Authors:     K. Moriarty, S. Farrell
  Stream/WG:   IETF, TLS Working Group

  Decisive text (RFC 8996, Abstract):

    "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS)
     versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those
     documents have been moved to Historic status."

  Restated in Section 1 (Introduction):

    "Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1
     [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008, which has
     now itself been superseded by TLS 1.3 [RFC8446]. Datagram Transport
     Layer Security (DTLS) version 1.0 [RFC4347] was superseded by DTLS
     1.2 [RFC6347] in 2012. Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate
     TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0. Accordingly, the aforementioned
     documents have been moved to Historic status."

2. THE STATUS GIVEN TO THE DEFINING RFCs

  RFC 2246 (The TLS Protocol Version 1.0)  ->  moved to Historic
  RFC 4346 (The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.1)  ->  moved to Historic

  The exact disposition is "moved to Historic status", i.e. the IETF
  document status classification for each of those RFCs changed from
  Proposed Standard to Historic. This is a status change of the documents
  themselves, not merely a statement that the protocols are "not
  recommended".

3. SCOPE OF THE SAME DISPOSITION (for completeness, not asked)

  RFC 8996 applies the same Historic move to:
    - RFC 4347 (Datagram TLS 1.0) — deprecated; DTLS 1.2 (RFC 6347) is not.
    - RFC 5469 (DES and IDEA cipher suites for TLS) — "since the only
      versions of TLS for which their usage is defined are now Historic,
      [RFC5469] has been moved to Historic as well."
  It also updates numerous RFCs that normatively reference TLS 1.0/1.1
  (e.g. RFC 6614's "TLS 1.1 or later" requirement becomes "TLS 1.2 or
  later"; RFC 7507's fallback SCSV is made moot by TLS 1.3's
  ServerHello.Random sentinel mechanism), and it reiterates the Historic
  status of RFC 6460, RFC 4744 and RFC 4743.

4. TERMINOLOGY NOTE (why the question's wording matters)

  "Deprecates" and "obsoletes" are distinct in the RFC series. TLS 1.0 and
  TLS 1.1 were *obsoleted* (superseded) earlier — by RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2,
  2008) and then RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3, 2018) — but they were *deprecated*,
  with their defining RFCs moved to Historic, by RFC 8996. RFC 8996
  itself does not obsolete RFC 2246 or RFC 4346; it changes their status.

5. CITATIONS

  [RFC8996] Moriarty, K. and S. Farrell, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1",
            BCP 195, RFC 8996, DOI 10.17487/RFC8996, March 2021,
            <https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8996/>.
  [RFC2246] Dierks, T. and C. Allen, "The TLS Protocol Version 1.0",
            RFC 2246, DOI 10.17487/RFC2246, January 1999 (now Historic).
  [RFC4346] Dierks, T. and E. Rescorla, "The Transport Layer Security (TLS)
            Protocol Version 1.1", RFC 4346, DOI 10.17487/RFC4346,
            April 2006 (now Historic).

  Verification sources consulted: rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.html
  (Abstract, Section 1, Section 6, Status of This Memo), the inline-errata
  rendering of the same text, rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8996/, and
  datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8996/history/ (publication date and BCP
  association).

6. BOTTOM LINE

  RFC 8996, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1" (BCP 195, March 2021),
  formally deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 and moved the RFCs that defined
  them — RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 — to Historic status.

The US Social Security contribution and benefit base (the OASDI taxable maximum) for calendar year 2026 is $184,500.

That is the maximum amount of earnings per worker per year subject to the 6.2% employee and 6.2% employer Social Security payroll tax (12.4% for self-employment income). Wages and net self-employment income are combined against this single annual cap. The same $184,500 is also the maximum amount of annual earnings that can count in a Social Security benefit computation for 2026.

SOURCE BASIS (official, current)

1. SSA, 'Contribution and Benefit Base' (ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html): the annual table lists 2026 = $184,500 (2025 = $176,100; 2027 = $192,300).
2. Federal Register, 90 FR (doc. 2025-19763), published 2025-11-03, automatic determinations for 2026: 'The Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI) contribution and benefit base will be $184,500 for remuneration paid in 2026 and self-employment income earned in tax years beginning in 2026.'
3. SSA Publication No. 05-10003 (2026 update): 'Social Security taxes ... Employee/employer (each) 6.2% on earnings up to $184,500'; 'Self-employed 12.4% on earnings up to $184,500' (2025 column: $176,100).
4. IRS Topic No. 751, 'Social Security and Medicare withholding rates': 'Only the Social Security tax has a wage base limit ... For earnings in 2026, this base limit is $184,500.'

HOW THE 2026 FIGURE IS DERIVED (statutory check)

Authority: Section 230(b) of the Social Security Act, as amended. The base for year Y after 1994 equals the 1994 base ($60,600) multiplied by the ratio of the national average wage index for year (Y-2) to that for 1992, rounded to the nearest multiple of $300, and never reduced below the prior year's base.

  2024 average wage index: $69,846.57
  1992 average wage index: $22,935.42
  $60,600 x (69,846.57 / 22,935.42) = $184,548.71
  Rounded to nearest $300 = $184,500
  $184,500 > 2025 base of $176,100, so the computed amount takes effect.

Result: $184,500 for 2026. The formula was applicable because a cost-of-living increase is effective for December 2025.

PAYROLL CONSEQUENCES AT THE 2026 CAP

  Employee:      6.2% x $184,500 = $11,439.00 maximum withheld
  Employer:      6.2% x $184,500 = $11,439.00 maximum (matching)
  Combined:     12.4% x $184,500 = $22,878.00
  Self-employed: 12.4% x $184,500 = $22,878.00 (before the income-tax deduction for one-half of SE tax)

Change from 2025: $184,500 - $176,100 = $8,400, an increase of 4.77%.

BOUNDARIES AND COMMON CONFLATIONS (stated so the number is not misapplied)

- Medicare / Hospital Insurance (HI) has NO earnings cap. The 1.45% employee + 1.45% employer (2.9% self-employed) HI tax applies to all covered wages, plus the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax above $200,000 of wages (employer withholding threshold, no employer match). Do not apply $184,500 to Medicare.
- $184,500 is the 2026 figure only. The 2027 base is $192,300 ($60,600 x 72,800.33 / 22,935.42 = $192,353.14, rounded). Do not use $192,300 for 2026.
- The 'old-law' contribution and benefit base for 2026 is a different, smaller figure: $137,100. It is used for Railroad Retirement tier II, PBGC guarantee limits, special-minimum-benefit years of coverage, and certain pension-offset computations — not for the payroll tax cap.
- Other 2026 annually adjusted amounts that are NOT the base and should not be substituted for it: retirement earnings test exempt amounts $24,480/yr (under NRA) and $65,160/yr (year of NRA), or $2,040 and $5,430 per month in the Federal Register formulation; quarter of coverage $1,890; PIA bend points $1,286 and $7,749; maximum-family-benefit bend points $1,643 / $2,371 / $3,093.
- The base applies to each worker individually, not per household, and to the sum of wage and self-employment earnings in the year; excess wage withholding is not automatically refunded by the employer but is reconciled on the individual's return.

One-line answer: $184,500 for 2026.

## Answer

**$24,500** — the 2026 limit on an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan, before any catch-up contribution (IRC §402(g)(1)).

This is the published statutory figure, not a projection.

## Authority

| Source | Statement |
|---|---|
| IRS Notice 2025-67 (2026 COLA notice, IRB 2025-49 at 761) | "The limitation under section 402(g)(1) on the exclusion for elective deferrals described in section 402(g)(3), which includes elective deferrals made to the Thrift Savings Plan, is increased from $23,500 to $24,500." |
| IRS, Retirement Topics – 401(k) and Profit-Sharing Plan Contribution Limits | "The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments." |
| IRS, Retirement Topics – Contributions | "The basic limit on elective deferrals is $24,500 in 2026 ... or 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less." |
| IRS, COLA Increases for Dollar Limitations (2026 column) | Elective deferrals: 24,500 |
| IRS Pub. 560 | "The basic limit on elective deferrals is $23,500 for 2025 and increases to $24,500 for 2026." |

Notice 2025-67 is the controlling guidance; the web pages and Pub. 560 restate it.

## What the $24,500 does and does not cover

**Included (all count against the single $24,500 cap):**
- Pre-tax (traditional) elective deferrals.
- Designated Roth elective deferrals — Roth 401(k) deferrals share the same §402(g) cap; electing Roth does not create additional room.
- Deferrals to any other §402(g) plan of the same employee in the same calendar year — 401(k), 403(b), SARSEP, and (for §402(g) aggregation purposes) other elective deferral arrangements. Deferrals are aggregated across all such plans and employers; the $24,500 is a per-employee annual ceiling, not a per-plan ceiling.

**Excluded from the $24,500:**
- Catch-up contributions (age 50+): $8,000 for 2026, permitted in addition to the base limit — total $32,500.
- The higher SECURE 2.0 catch-up for participants who attain age 60, 61, 62, or 63 in 2026: $11,250 — total $35,750. (Unchanged from 2025.)
- Employer matching, nonelective, and profit-sharing contributions — governed by the §415(c) annual additions limit, $72,000 for 2026.
- SIMPLE 401(k) deferrals — a separate limit of $17,000 for 2026; the $24,500 figure does **not** apply to a SIMPLE 401(k).
- Section 457(b) deferrals — a parallel $24,500 limit under §457(e)(15), with its own aggregation rules.

## Applying it in payroll for 2026

1. Set the annual employee deferral election cap at $24,500 for pre-tax plus Roth combined, per employee, across all §402(g) plans.
2. Apply the compensation floor: the effective limit is the lesser of $24,500 or 100% of the employee's compensation. An employee earning under $24,500 for the year cannot reach $24,500.
3. Do not reduce the $24,500 by employer match or nonelective contributions; those are tested separately against §72,000.
4. Where an employee participates in more than one §402(g) plan (e.g., a prior employer's 401(k) earlier in the year, or a 403(b) alongside the 401(k)), collect a deferral-history certification and reduce the remaining election room accordingly.
5. Check the plan document and any nondiscrimination testing outcome: plan terms may impose a lower cap (e.g., a percentage-of-compensation limit), and ADP/ACP testing or a §414(v) plan limit can further restrict a highly compensated employee below $24,500. The statutory figure is a ceiling, never a floor.
6. Excess deferrals above $24,500 (aggregate) are includible in gross income for the year and must be corrected under EPCRS; distribute by April 15 of the following year to avoid double taxation.

## Caveats worth stating alongside the number

- Figure is for the **calendar tax year 2026**. A non-calendar plan year spanning 2025–2026 uses the limit of the calendar year in which the deferral is made.
- Figure is in **whole U.S. dollars**, rounded per the statutory indexing convention (nearest multiple of $500 for §402(g)).
- The 2026 figure is final as published in Notice 2025-67. Subsequent legislation could change it prospectively; confirm against Notice 2025-67 or any later IRS guidance before locking payroll configuration.

answer:
# Current US National Primary Ambient Air Quality Standards for PM2.5

## Answer

| Averaging time | Primary standard level | Form of the standard |
|---|---|---|
| Annual | **9.0 µg/m³** (micrograms per cubic meter), annual arithmetic mean concentration | Met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration, determined per appendix N to 40 CFR part 50, is **less than or equal to 9.0 µg/m³** |
| 24-hour | **35 µg/m³**, 24-hour average concentration | Met when the 98th percentile 24-hour concentration, determined per appendix N to 40 CFR part 50, is **less than or equal to 35 µg/m³** |

Both are measured in the ambient air as PM2.5 (particles with an aerodynamic diameter less than or equal to a nominal 2.5 micrometers) by a reference method based on appendix L to 40 CFR part 50 and designated under part 53, or by an equivalent method designated under part 53.

## Authority and currency

- **Codified at:** 40 CFR § 50.20 — "National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5," paragraphs (a), (b) and (c).
- **Source of the current levels:** 89 FR 16380 (Mar. 6, 2024) — *Reconsideration of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter* (signed Feb. 7, 2024; effective 60 days after publication, May 6, 2024).
- **Currency check:** the electronic Code of Federal Regulations text of § 50.20 carries no amendment later than 89 FR 16380; the annual level was lowered from 12.0 µg/m³ to 9.0 µg/m³ by that rule and the 24-hour level was retained unchanged at 35 µg/m³. EPA's NAAQS-for-PM page confirms the same two facts ("setting the level of the primary (health-based) annual PM2.5 standard at 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter" and "EPA is not changing the current: primary and secondary (welfare-based) 24-hour PM2.5 standards").

## Text of the controlling provision (verbatim, § 50.20(a)–(c))

> (a) The national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration measured in the ambient air as PM2.5 ...
>
> (b) The primary annual PM2.5 standard is met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N to this part, is less than or equal to 9.0 µg/m3.
>
> (c) The primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard is met when the 98th percentile 24-hour concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N to this part, is less than or equal to 35 µg/m3.

## Reporting conventions to preserve

- Write the annual level as **9.0 µg/m³** — the trailing decimal is part of the regulatory statement of the level; do not shorten it to "9 µg/m³" in a regulatory context.
- Write the 24-hour level as **35 µg/m³** — stated as an integer, with no decimal.
- The unit symbol in the CFR text is rendered "µg/m3"; "µg/m³" is the same unit and is acceptable in narrative use.
- Compliance is a "less than or equal to" comparison against the stated level after the appendix N data handling (3-year averaging of annual means for the annual standard; 3-year average of annual 98th-percentile 24-hour values for the 24-hour standard) and appendix N rounding. The numeric levels above are the comparison values, not raw unrounded monitoring results.

## Do not confuse these with other PM2.5 provisions still in Part 50

The following appear in the same part and are **not** the current primary standards; they remain codified for older designations and continuing implementation obligations:

| Provision | Annual | 24-hour | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| § 50.20 (2024 reconsideration) | 9.0 µg/m³ | 35 µg/m³ | **Current primary standards — the answer** |
| § 50.18 (2012 review) | 12.0 µg/m³ | 35 µg/m³ | Superseded annual level; the 2012 primary annual standard remains relevant to areas designated under it |
| § 50.13 (1997/2006 review) | 15.0 µg/m³ | 35 µg/m³ | 1997 primary annual standard revoked for most purposes per § 50.13(d); 1997 secondary annual and 1997 24-hour standards remain in effect |

## Scope note (primary vs. secondary)

This answer covers the **primary** (health-based) standards, as asked. For completeness: the secondary (welfare-based) 24-hour PM2.5 standard is also 35 µg/m³, while the secondary annual PM2.5 standard was retained at 15.0 µg/m³ in the 2024 rule and was not changed to 9.0 µg/m³.

## Status watch

EPA announced on March 12, 2025 a "path forward" on the PM2.5 standards (reconsideration). As of the eCFR text cited above, § 50.20 still reads 9.0 µg/m³ annual and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour, with no later amendment. If a future rulemaking revises § 50.20, the annual figure is the one that would move; the 24-hour figure has been 35 µg/m³ since 2006.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 9.0 on ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-i/subchapter-c/part-50/section-50.20 and 15.0 on ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-i/subchapter-c/part-50/section-50.13. The first reads: "(b) The primary annual PM2.5 standard is met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N to this part, is less than or equal to 9.0 µg/m3."

question: M4
answer:
ANSWER

4 feet (1.2 m) above a lower level.

Under the OSHA general-industry walking-working surfaces standard, an employer must protect each employee on a walking-working surface that has an unprotected side or edge and that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level. This is the general rule of 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i); 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(15) ('Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed') sets the same 4-foot (1.2 m) trigger for surfaces not covered by a more specific paragraph.

1. REGULATORY BASIS

Standard: 29 CFR Part 1910, Subpart D — Walking-Working Surfaces.
Governing paragraph: 1910.28(b)(1)(i) — 'The employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by one or more of the following: (A) Guardrail systems; (B) Safety net systems; or (C) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems.'
Residual paragraph: 1910.28(b)(15) — same 4 feet (1.2 m) trigger, protection by guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall protection systems.

This is a general-industry rule. It does not apply to construction work, which is governed by 29 CFR Part 1926, Subpart M, where the corresponding trigger for unprotected sides and edges is 6 feet (1.8 m) (1926.501(b)(1)). Because the question is expressly 'general industry, not construction,' the correct number is 4 feet, not 6 feet.

2. HOW TO APPLY THE 4-FOOT TRIGGER

- Measure vertically from the walking-working surface on which the employee stands to the next lower level. If that distance is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more, protection is required.
- 'Unprotected side or edge' means an edge without a guardrail system, safety net system, or personal fall protection system meeting 1910.29 criteria. A guardrail that does not meet 1910.29(b) (e.g., top rail below 39 inches (99 cm), or a rail that does not withstand the 200-pound (890 N) load) does not remove the exposure.
- The 4-foot trigger is a floor, not a target. An employer may impose a lower internal trigger (many do, e.g., 4 feet everywhere, or 100% tie-off), and a state-plan state may set a stricter requirement; neither changes the federal minimum.
- No hazard assessment, 'competent person' determination, or feasibility finding is needed to trigger the duty. The duty attaches at 4 feet (1.2 m) by rule. (The only route to an alternative is the fall protection plan option in 1910.28(b)(1)(ii), discussed in section 5.)

3. WHAT COUNTS AS PROTECTION AT OR ABOVE 4 FEET

Any one or more of the following, each built and used per 1910.29:
- Guardrail system (1910.29(b)): top rail 39-45 inches (99-114 cm), midrail, 200 lb (890 N) load capacity, etc.
- Safety net system (1910.29(c)).
- Personal fall protection system (1910.29(d)-(f), 1910.140): personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning system.

Note that for the general walking-working surface case, a warning line alone, a designated area alone, or a cover is not listed as an acceptable substitute in 1910.28(b)(1)(i). Covers are the control for holes (1910.28(b)(3)); designated areas and warning lines appear only in specific paragraphs (e.g., low-slope roofs).

4. SPECIAL CASES — OTHER PARAGRAPHS OF 1910.28(b) THAT SET THEIR OWN TRIGGER

These do not change the general answer; they show where a different paragraph displaces 1910.28(b)(1)(i). All values below are as they appear in the regulatory text.

| Condition (1910.28(b) paragraph) | Trigger | Permitted protection |
|---|---|---|
| Hoist areas (b)(2) | 4 ft (1.2 m) or more | Guardrail, personal fall arrest, or travel restraint; personal fall arrest required when leaning through/over the edge with guardrail, gate, or chain removed |
| Holes, including skylights (b)(3)(i) | 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above a lower level | Covers, guardrail, travel restraint, or personal fall arrest |
| Holes less than 4 ft (1.2 m) above a lower level (b)(3)(ii) | any depth below 4 ft | Covers or guardrail systems (trip/step-in hazard) |
| Dangerous equipment (b)(6)(i) | employee less than 4 ft (1.2 m) above dangerous equipment | Guardrail or travel restraint, unless the equipment is covered or guarded to eliminate the hazard |
| Dangerous equipment (b)(6)(ii) | 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above dangerous equipment | Guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or personal fall arrest |
| Stairway landings (b)(11)(i) | 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above a lower level | Guardrail or stair rail system |
| Rope descent systems (b)(12)(ii) | 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above a lower level | Personal fall arrest system |
| Slaughtering facility platforms (b)(14)(i) | 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above a lower level | Guardrail or travel restraint; infeasibility exception with limited access and 1910.30 training |
| Fixed ladders (b)(9) | extends more than 24 ft (7.3 m) above a lower level | Ladder safety system or personal fall arrest system — this is a separate requirement keyed to 24 ft, not a substitute for the 4-ft walking-working-surface trigger |
| Scaffolds (b)(12)(i) | incorporated by reference | Protection per 29 CFR Part 1926, Subpart L (construction scaffold rule), not the 1910.28(b)(1)(i) list |
| Low-slope roofs (b)(13) | keyed to distance from the roof edge, not height | Less than 6 ft (1.6 m) from edge: guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or personal fall arrest. At least 6 ft (1.6 m) but less than 15 ft (4.6 m): same, or a designated area if the work is infrequent and temporary. 15 ft (4.6 m) or more: same, or a designated area; no fall protection required if the work is both infrequent and temporary, plus a work rule prohibiting employees within 15 ft (4.6 m) of the edge without fall protection |

Note on the low-slope roof rows: 6 ft and 15 ft there are horizontal distances from the roof edge, not heights above a lower level. They are not competing answers to the question asked.

5. EXCEPTION ROUTE — FALL PROTECTION PLAN

1910.28(b)(1)(ii) permits an employer that can demonstrate that use of guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall protection systems is not feasible or would create a greater hazard to instead develop and implement a written fall protection plan meeting 1910.29(k). This exception is not available for work on low-slope roofs. If an employer relies on it, the written plan — not the 4-foot trigger — becomes the compliance artifact, and the employer bears the burden of the demonstration.

6. DUTIES THAT TRAVEL WITH THE TRIGGER

- Training: employees exposed to fall hazards must be trained per 1910.30 (nature of hazards, procedures, and the systems in use); retraining when the workplace or systems change or when an employee shows inadequate understanding.
- Equipment: fall protection systems must meet 1910.29 criteria and be inspected per 1910.29 (guardrails, covers, and personal fall protection equipment before each use, per 1910.140 for personal fall arrest systems).
- Personal fall arrest systems: rigged so total fall distance and swing fall are controlled; prompt rescue of an employee after a fall is required (1910.140).
- Falling objects: where employees are exposed to falling objects, head protection per Subpart I plus one or more of toeboards/screens/guardrails, canopy structures, or barricading (1910.28(c)).

7. CAVEATS A COMPETENT ENGINEER SHOULD STATE ALONGSIDE THE NUMBER

- State-plan states: 29 CFR 1910 is the federal floor. Roughly half the states and territories operate OSHA-approved state plans that must be at least as effective as the federal standard and may be stricter. Confirm the site's state-plan rule before fixing a single corporate trigger. The 4-foot federal value is the correct answer to the question as asked (US federal general industry).
- Construction vs. general industry: maintenance work on a building can flip parts of a job into Part 1926 (6-foot trigger, plus 1926.501(b)(1) and the 1926.502 criteria). Classify the work, then pick the part.
- 'Lower level' can be a floor, a platform, a pit, a piece of equipment, or grade. The measurement is to the surface the employee would strike, not to the nearest structural member.
- Do not read the 24-foot fixed-ladder figure as the fall-protection trigger. It governs when a ladder safety system or personal fall arrest system is required on a fixed ladder; the 4-foot trigger still governs walking-working surfaces generally.

BOTTOM LINE

4 feet (1.2 m). Cite 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) (general rule) and 1910.28(b)(15) (surfaces not otherwise addressed). Protect by guardrail system, safety net system, or personal fall protection system meeting 1910.29, train per 1910.30, and check the governing state plan for any stricter trigger.

question: M6
answer:
**Answer.** The legal minimum reserve fuel for a civil helicopter beginning a VFR flight in the United States is **20 minutes** of flight at normal cruising speed, after reaching the first point of intended landing. This is the same for day and night VFR.

**Primary rule (Part 91).** 14 CFR 91.151(b): No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes. Helicopters are rotorcraft, so 20 minutes applies. The airplane-specific 30-minute day / 45-minute night reserve in 91.151(a) does not apply to helicopters.

**Part 135.** If the flight is conducted under Part 135, 14 CFR 135.209(b) imposes the same 20-minute helicopter VFR reserve; FAA guidance confirms that during day or night the required reserve is 20 minutes. Thus the answer does not change between Part 91 and Part 135 for helicopter VFR.

**What the reserve is not.** It is not a fixed gallon quantity. It is a time reserve at normal cruising speed/fuel consumption. The 30-minute helicopter figure appears only in IFR rules (91.167(a)(3) and 135.223(a)(3), after alternate fuel where required), not in VFR helicopter rules.

**Computation.** Required reserve volume = normal cruise fuel burn rate in usable fuel volume per hour multiplied by 20/60 hour, i.e. burn rate x 0.3333 hour. Total fuel at start must be at least: taxi/startup allowance + fuel to first point of intended landing + 20-minute reserve + any operational contingency the pilot adds. Example only: at 90 gal/h normal cruise, 20 minutes = 30 gal. Use the helicopter POH/AFM and planned cruise, with wind and forecast weather considered.

**Operational note.** The 20 minutes is a legal floor, not a prudent flight-planning reserve. Pilots commonly carry additional fuel for weather, routing, delays, and diversion. But the regulatory minimum beyond the first landing point is 20 minutes.

1. The RFC that deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 is RFC 8996, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1" (K. Moriarty, S. Farrell; March 2021; 18 pages; DOI 10.17487/RFC8996; published as an Internet Best Current Practice and part of BCP 195; produced by the TLS working group from draft-ietf-tls-oldversions-deprecate-12).

2. The status it gave the RFCs that defined those versions — RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0) and RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1) — is Historic. It did not replace them with a new protocol specification; it moved the existing documents to Historic, i.e. deprecated without a successor document.

PRIMARY EVIDENCE (quoted verbatim)

RFC 8996 abstract: "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."

RFC 8996, Section 1 (Introduction): "Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1 [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008, which has now itself been superseded by TLS 1.3 [RFC8446]. Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) version 1.0 [RFC4347] was superseded by DTLS 1.2 [RFC6347] in 2012. Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0. Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to Historic status."

RFC 8996, "Status of This Memo": "This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice." (RFC 8996's own status is Best Current Practice — it is not itself Historic; the Historic status applies to the documents it deprecates.)

RFC 8996 JSON metadata: pub_status/status = BEST CURRENT PRACTICE; pub_date March 2021; obsoletes RFC5469 and RFC7507; updates a long list including RFC3261, RFC5246-adjacent protocol RFCs, RFC6347, RFC7525, RFC8422.

SCOPE OF THE STATUS CHANGE (for precision)

- RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0) -> Historic.
- RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1) -> Historic.
- RFC 4347 (DTLS 1.0) -> also deprecated and moved to Historic, per the abstract: "This document also deprecates Datagram TLS (DTLS) version 1.0 (RFC 4347) but not DTLS version 1.2, and there is no DTLS version 1.1."
- RFC 5469 (DES/IDEA cipher suites) -> RFC 8996 states it "has been moved to Historic as well"; the document's own metadata also lists RFC 5469 under "obsoletes".
- RFC 7507 (TLS Fallback SCSV) -> its functionality "has been superseded" by the TLS 1.3 ServerHello.Random mechanism, and RFC 8996 lists RFC 7507 under "obsoletes" (i.e. Obsoleted, not Historic).
- RFC 7525 (TLS best practices) -> updated, not deprecated; RFC 8996 thereby becomes part of BCP 195.
- Many RFCs that normatively reference TLS 1.0/1.1 are updated (the metadata lists roughly 90 "updates" entries); several already-Historic or already-obsoleted RFCs are listed as updated merely to reiterate that modern TLS must be used.

DISTINCTION THE QUESTION TURNS ON

"Obsoleted" means replaced by a newer specification; "Historic" means the specification is no longer recommended and has been retired, with no same-protocol successor document. RFC 8996 performs the latter for RFC 2246 and RFC 4346. (TLS 1.2/RFC 5246 and TLS 1.3/RFC 8446 are the protocol successors in a practical sense, and RFC 4346 had already obsoleted RFC 2246 and been obsoleted by RFC 5246 in the RFC index; but the formal status label assigned to RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 by the deprecating document is Historic.)

VERIFICATION TABLE

| Item | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Deprecating RFC | RFC 8996 | rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8996/, rfc8996.html, rfc8996.xml, rfc8996.json |
| Title | Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 | rfc8996.json |
| Publication date | March 2021 | rfc8996.json |
| RFC 8996's own status | Best Current Practice (BCP 195) | rfc8996.json; Status of This Memo |
| Status assigned to RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0) | Historic | abstract and Section 1 |
| Status assigned to RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1) | Historic | abstract and Section 1 |
| Status assigned to RFC 4347 (DTLS 1.0) | Historic | abstract and Section 1 |
| RFCs obsoleted by RFC 8996 | RFC 5469, RFC 7507 | rfc8996.json "obsoletes" |

CONSISTENCY NOTE

No numeric thresholds or computed figures appear in this deliverable, so no value can violate a stated bound. The only repeated values are the identifiers RFC 8996, RFC 2246, RFC 4346 and the status word Historic; they are identical in the results list, the answer, and the evidence quotes.

The US Social Security contribution and benefit base (the OASDI taxable maximum) for calendar year 2026 is $184,500.

This is the maximum amount of earnings subject to the 6.2% employee and 6.2% employer Social Security payroll tax in 2026, and it is simultaneously the maximum amount of annual earnings creditable toward Social Security benefit computation for 2026. It applies to remuneration paid in 2026 and to self-employment income earned in tax years beginning in 2026.

STATUS: FINAL / OFFICIALLY DETERMINED, not a projection. The figure was announced in the fall of 2025 and published in the Federal Register on November 3, 2025 (90 FR 49047, document 2025-19763).

1. THE VALUE AND ITS IMMEDIATE COROLLARIES

  Contribution and benefit base (OASDI taxable maximum), 2026: $184,500
  Employee OASDI rate: 6.2% -> maximum employee withholding 2026 = 0.062 x 184,500 = $11,439.00
  Employer OASDI rate: 6.2% -> maximum employer contribution 2026 = $11,439.00
  Self-employed OASDI rate: 12.4% -> maximum self-employment OASDI tax 2026 = 0.124 x 184,500 = $22,878.00
  Combined employee + employer at the cap: $22,878.00
  Medicare (HI) 2026: NO wage cap; 1.45% each on all earnings, 2.9% self-employed, plus the 0.9% additional Medicare tax above the statutory threshold. The $184,500 does not apply to Medicare.
  Prior year (2025) base: $176,100 -> 2026 increase: $8,400, or 4.77%.
  'Old-law' contribution and benefit base for 2026: $137,100 (a separate, lower series used for Railroad Retirement, PBGC guarantee limits, special-minimum year-of-coverage determinations, and certain non-covered-pension benefit computations; it is NOT the payroll-tax cap and must not be substituted for $184,500).

2. STATUTORY DERIVATION (verification of the published number)

Authority: Section 230(b) of the Social Security Act. The base for 2026 is the larger of:
  (1) the 1994 base ($60,600) multiplied by the ratio of the national average wage index (NAWI) for 2024 to the NAWI for 1992, rounded to the nearest multiple of $300; or
  (2) the current base ($176,100).

Inputs (as determined by SSA and published in the same Federal Register notice):
  NAWI 2024 = $69,846.57
  NAWI 1992 = $22,935.42
  Ratio = 69,846.57 / 22,935.42 = 3.045358 (to 6 dp)

Computation:
  60,600 x 3.045358 = $184,548.71
  Round to nearest multiple of $300: 184,548.71 / 300 = 615.1624 -> 615; 615 x 300 = $184,500
  Test against the current base: $184,500 > $176,100, so the formula result governs and the 2026 base is $184,500.

This reproduces the published figure exactly and confirms the internal consistency of the value with the stated NAWI inputs and the $300 rounding rule.

3. SOURCE TRAIL (all primary, all SSA or Federal Register)

  a) SSA, 'Contribution and Benefit Base' table (ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html): 2025 = $176,100; 2026 = $184,500; 2027 = $192,300. Same page restates that the limit applies both to taxation and to benefit computation and changes annually with the national average wage index.
  b) Federal Register, 90 FR 49047 (Nov. 3, 2025), 'Determination of the OASDI Contribution and Benefit Base for 2026': '(1) The Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI) contribution and benefit base will be $184,500 for remuneration paid in 2026 and self-employment income earned in tax years beginning in 2026.' Same notice gives the computation reproduced in section 2 above.
  c) SSA, Detailed Calculator update page (ssa.gov/oact/anypia/update.html): 'Contribution and benefit base for 2026: $184,500'; also 'Old-law contribution and benefit base for 2026: $137,100' and 'Cost-of-living adjustment for December 2025: 2.8 percent.'

question: M12
answer:
ANSWER

2026 elective deferral limit for a 401(k) plan, before any catch-up contribution: $24,500.

This is the IRC §402(g)(1) limit as adjusted for cost of living, announced in IRS Notice 2025-67 (up from $23,500 for 2025). It is the base limit for a participant who makes no catch-up contributions.

AUTHORITY (all three agree)
- IRS Notice 2025-67: "The limitation under section 402(g)(1) on the exclusion for elective deferrals ... is increased from $23,500 to $24,500."
- IRS, Retirement topics — 401(k) and profit-sharing plan contribution limits: "The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments."
- IRS Publication 560: "The limit on elective deferrals, other than catch-up contributions, is $23,500 for 2025 and $24,500 for 2026."

SCOPE CONDITIONS THAT MUST TRAVEL WITH THE NUMBER
1. Plan type. $24,500 applies to standard 401(k) plans, including traditional and safe harbor 401(k) designs, and also to SARSEPs, 403(b) plans and governmental 457(b) plans. It does NOT apply to a SIMPLE 401(k), whose 2026 limit is $17,000.
2. Per individual, not per plan. The limit is applied to the aggregate of elective deferrals the individual makes across all plans of the same employer and its controlled group/affiliated service group. Two plans of one employer do not give two $24,500 buckets.
3. Pre-tax and Roth share one limit. Traditional (pre-tax) elective deferrals and designated Roth elective deferrals are counted together against the single $24,500 ceiling; electing Roth does not create additional room.
4. Catch-up sits on top and is excluded here. Age 50+ catch-up for 2026 is $8,000 (total $32,500 for a participant using the full base plus catch-up); the SECURE 2.0 age 60–63 "super catch-up" is $11,250 (total $35,750). Neither is part of the $24,500 figure.
5. The $24,500 is a ceiling, not an entitlement. A plan document may impose a lower dollar or percentage cap, and nondiscrimination testing (ADP test under §401(k)(3)) or the §415(c) annual additions limit ($72,000 for 2026, inclusive of employer contributions and forfeitures but excluding catch-up) can reduce the amount an individual can actually defer. Where a plan limit or ADP limit binds, deferrals above that lower amount are treated as catch-up contributions for a participant eligible to make them, and otherwise are excess deferrals.
6. Compensation limit. Compensation taken into account for 2026 is capped at $360,000; this does not change the $24,500 dollar limit but will bind percentage-based plan formulas for high earners.
7. Not in scope: the SECURE 2.0 Roth catch-up requirement for employees with prior-year FICA wages above $150,000 (for 2026) applies only to catch-up contributions and does not alter the base $24,500 limit.

CORRECTION MECHANICS (if the limit is exceeded)
Excess deferrals above $24,500 (aggregated across the employer's plans) are includible in gross income for the year of deferral. If distributed by April 15 of the following year, earnings are taxed in the year of distribution and the excess is not double-taxed; if not timely distributed, the amount is taxed twice. Plan-level correction follows EPCRS.

QUICK REFERENCE — 2026 401(k) FIGURES
- Base elective deferral limit (§402(g)): $24,500
- Age 50+ catch-up: $8,000
- Age 60–63 catch-up: $11,250
- §415(c) annual additions: $72,000
- Compensation limit (§401(a)(17)): $360,000
- SIMPLE 401(k) deferral limit: $17,000 (SIMPLE catch-up $4,000; age 60–63 SIMPLE catch-up $5,250)

# Current US National Primary Ambient Air Quality Standards for PM2.5

## 1. Answer

| Pollutant / averaging time | Primary standard level | Statistical form (regulatory) | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| PM2.5, annual | **9.0 µg/m³** | Annual arithmetic mean concentration, averaged over 3 years; standard is met when the 3-year average annual arithmetic mean is ≤ 9.0 µg/m³ | 40 CFR 50.20(a), (b) |
| PM2.5, 24-hour | **35 µg/m³** | 98th percentile of 24-hour concentrations, averaged over 3 years; standard is met when the 3-year average of annual 98th percentiles is ≤ 35 µg/m³ | 40 CFR 50.20(a), (c) |

Both are **primary** (health-based) standards under Clean Air Act § 109. Units are micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³) of PM2.5 in ambient air, measured by a reference method (appendix L / part 53) or an equivalent method (part 53).

## 2. Source reconciliation — why two different annual numbers appear in the CFR

The retrieved sources show two annual figures (12.0 and 9.0). This is not a conflict in the current standard; it is the normal EPA codification pattern of leaving a superseded standard in place in its own section:

- **40 CFR 50.20** — “National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 … are 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³) annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour average concentration … (b) … met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration … is less than or equal to 9.0 µg/m³. (c) … met when the 98th percentile 24-hour concentration … is less than or equal to 35 µg/m³.” This is the standard established by EPA’s 2024 reconsideration of the PM NAAQS and is the **current** standard.
- **40 CFR 50.18** — the 2012 review standard: 12.0 µg/m³ annual, 35 µg/m³ 24-hour, `[78 FR 3277, Jan. 15, 2013]`. It remains in the CFR as the prior standard; it is **not** the current annual level.

Independent corroboration from the EPA rule-summary page and the EPA “PM NAAQS Overview” fact sheet (Feb 2024): “EPA is setting the level of the primary (health-based) annual PM2.5 standard at 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter”; “EPA is revising the level of the primary (health-based) annual PM2.5 standard from 12.0 µg/m³ to 9.0 µg/m³”; “EPA is retaining the primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard at the level of 35 µg/m³.” The fact sheet’s standards table lists: PM2.5 annual, primary 9.0 µg/m³ (secondary 15.0 µg/m³), form “annual arithmetic mean, averaged over 3 years”; PM2.5 24-hour, primary and secondary 35 µg/m³, form “98th percentile, averaged over 3 years.”

The 24-hour answer is unaffected by which section governs: 35 µg/m³ under both 50.18 and 50.20, because the 2024 action retained that standard unchanged.

## 3. Primary vs. secondary — keep the distinction explicit

The request is limited to **primary** standards. For completeness of context only (not part of the answer): the secondary (welfare-based) PM2.5 standards are 15.0 µg/m³ annual (unchanged in 2024) and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour. The secondary annual level is therefore *higher* (less stringent) than the primary annual level — do not substitute it. The 24-hour primary and secondary levels happen to be identical (35 µg/m³).

## 4. Currency, date stamp, and what would change this answer

- **As-of date of the values above: 2026-11-17** (retrieval date of the codified text and EPA pages used). The CFR edition consulted carries a Jan 27, 2026 typesetting stamp and still reads 9.0 / 35 at 50.20.
- **Open watch item:** the EPA PM NAAQS page displays a **2025-03-12** notice, “Trump EPA Announces Path Forward on National Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter (PM2.5)…”, alongside the 2024 final rule. No final rule changing the codified levels is reflected in the text retrieved on 2026-11-17. A subsequent final rule (or a court vacatur of the 2024 reconsideration) would change the annual answer; the 24-hour answer would change only if the retained 35 µg/m³ were reopened.
- **Verification procedure for a downstream reviewer:** (a) pull 40 CFR 50.20 from eCFR (current) or the current annual CFR volume; (b) confirm paragraph (a) levels and paragraphs (b)/(c) “met when ≤” thresholds; (c) cross-check against the EPA “National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) for PM” page rule summary; (d) if 50.18 and 50.20 both appear, use the highest-numbered PM2.5 primary section as current and treat earlier sections as prior standards.

## 5. Compliance notes (form, not just level)

1. **The level is not the compliance test by itself.** Attainment is judged on the appendix N statistics: the 3-year average of annual arithmetic means (annual standard) and the 3-year average of annual 98th-percentile 24-hour values (24-hour standard). A single year above 9.0 or above 35 does not by itself constitute nonattainment.
2. **Data completeness and rounding** are governed by appendix N and the general provisions of 40 CFR Part 50 (commonly applied: 75% quarterly data capture per year, and rounding of the 3-year statistic before comparison to the level). Read the appendix N text and Part 50 general provisions for the controlling wording before making a design-value or attainment determination; those procedural provisions are not reproduced here.
3. **Two PM2.5 primary sections coexist in the CFR.** Programs, permits, and State Implementation Plan obligations tied to the 2012 standard continue to reference 50.18 (12.0 µg/m³) for the areas and periods to which that standard applies, while the 2024 standard at 50.20 (9.0 µg/m³) governs going forward with its own designation and implementation schedule. When citing “the standard” in a permit or rule, cite the section that applies to the obligation at hand rather than assuming a single number governs everything.
4. **Scope limits of this answer:** it states the standards’ levels and forms. It does not state attainment/nonattainment designations, class areas, or state-specific implementation deadlines, which are separate determinations and are not derivable from the standard levels.
