question: M4
answer:
# Fall Protection Trigger Height — General Industry Walking-Working Surfaces with an Unprotected Side or Edge

## 1. Answer

**4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level.**

Under the federal OSHA general industry standard, an employer must protect an employee on a walking-working surface that has an unprotected side or edge when that surface is **4 feet or more above a lower level**. At exactly 4 ft 0 in the duty attaches; there is no tolerance band above 4 ft. Below 4 ft, this particular paragraph does not impose the duty (other requirements may still apply — see §6).

## 2. Controlling text

**29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i)** (current eCFR text, fetched 2026-11-17):

> "Except as provided elsewhere in this section, the employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by one or more of the following:
> (A) Guardrail systems;
> (B) Safety net systems; or
> (C) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems."

Definitions that drive application (1910.28(c) / Subpart D definitions):

- **Walking-working surface** — any horizontal or vertical surface on or through which an employee walks, works, or gains access to a work area or workplace location.
- **Unprotected sides and edges** — any side or edge of a walking-working surface (except at entrances and other points of access) where there is no wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system protecting an employee from falling to a lower level.
- **Lower level** — the surface below the walking-working surface onto which an employee would fall.

The same 4-foot trigger is repeated across the section, which confirms it is the general-industry baseline and not a paragraph-specific number:

| Paragraph | Subject | Trigger |
|---|---|---|
| 1910.28(b)(1)(i) | Unprotected sides and edges | **4 ft (1.2 m)** or more above a lower level |
| 1910.28(b)(11)(i) | Stairway landings (guardrail/stair rail) | **4 ft** or more above a lower level |
| 1910.28(b)(12)(ii) | Rope descent systems (PFAS) | **4 ft** or more above a lower level |
| 1910.28(b)(14)(i) | Slaughtering facility platforms | **4 ft** or more above a lower level |
| 1910.28(b)(15) | Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed | **4 ft** or more above a lower level |

## 3. Why 4 and not 6 — the regime question

- The 4-foot figure is the **general industry** number (29 CFR Part 1910, Subpart D).
- **Construction** uses a different number: 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1) requires conventional fall protection at **6 feet** above a lower level. That 6-foot figure is **not** the answer here; it is stated only to mark the boundary. If the same employee were engaged in construction work, Part 1926 would govern and the trigger would be 6 ft.
- Related maritime/longshoring regimes (Parts 1915, 1917, 1918) and the paragraph-specific carve-outs in 1910.28(a)(2) (powered platforms §1910.66(j); aerial lifts §1910.67(c)(2)(v); telecommunications §1910.268(n)(7)–(8); electric power §1910.269(g)(2)(i)) displace 1910.28 where they apply. For an ordinary general-industry walking-working surface, none of these applies.
- **State-plan jurisdictions:** 1910.28 is the federal floor. OSHA-approved State Plans must be at least as effective as federal but may be stricter, and the adopted text can differ. Example in hand: Oregon OSHA adopted 1910.28(b)(1)(i) with the same **4 ft (1.2 m)** trigger, but did **not** adopt paragraph (b)(1)(ii) or its note (the residential-roof fall-protection-plan option). **Action for the employer:** confirm which State Plan covers the workplace before relying on any exception; the 4-foot trigger is the value to carry into that check.

## 4. Exceptions and special rules — verify before relying on any of them

These do not raise the 4-foot trigger generally; they are narrow alternatives that must be affirmatively established and documented.

1. **Residential roofs — infeasibility/greater hazard** — 1910.28(b)(1)(ii): where the employer can demonstrate that guardrail, safety net, or personal fall protection systems are not feasible or create a greater hazard on residential roofs, the employer must develop and implement a fall protection plan meeting 29 CFR 1926.502(k) plus training per 1926.503(a) and (c). *Not adopted in Oregon.*
2. **Loading racks, loading docks, teeming platforms** — 1910.28(b)(1)(iii): where the employer can demonstrate fall protection systems are not feasible **on the working side** of such a platform, work may proceed without a fall protection system only if (A) the infeasible work operation is in process, (B) access to the platform is limited to authorized employees, and (C) those employees are trained per 1910.30.
3. **Slaughtering facility platforms** — 1910.28(b)(14): guardrail or travel restraint at 4 ft; if not feasible, work may proceed without them only with the in-process operation, limited authorized access, and 1910.30 training conditions of (b)(14)(ii).
4. **Low-slope roofs** — 1910.28(b)(13): a separate rule keyed to **horizontal distance from the roof edge**, not to height above a lower level — protection is required when work is performed **less than 6 ft (1.6 m)** from the edge, with the requirements tightening/loosening in the 6-to-under-15 ft band and at 15 ft (4.6 m) or more, and with a work rule barring employees from going within 15 ft (4.6 m) of the edge without fall protection. Do **not** read the 6 ft / 15 ft numbers as height triggers; they are edge distances. Confirm the current subparagraph allocation against the eCFR text before writing a site procedure against it.
5. **Scope carve-outs** — 1910.28(a)(2): the section does not apply to the specifically listed equipment/operations (powered platforms, aerial lifts, telecom, electric power) which have their own fall-protection provisions.

## 5. How to measure "4 feet above a lower level"

1. Identify the **lower level**: the surface, equipment, or bottom of the space onto which an employee would actually fall (floor, grade, mezzanine, pit bottom, tank interior, conveyor, etc.).
2. Measure **vertically** from the walking-working surface to that lower level. Do not measure from the top of an existing rail, from a toe board, or to the top of intervening equipment.
3. Where the drop varies along the edge, evaluate at the point of exposure — the duty attaches wherever any portion of the exposed edge is 4 ft or more above a lower level.
4. An **unprotected** side or edge exists only where there is no wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system; a compliant existing guardrail or wall removes the exposure (entrances and other access points are excluded from the definition).
5. Treat the 4 ft as a **trigger, not a target**: at or above 4 ft the protection must already be in place, not planned.

## 6. Compliance procedure for the employer

**Step 1 — Classify the work.** Confirm the activity is general industry (Part 1910) and not construction (Part 1926, 6 ft) or a maritime regime. Document the basis.
**Step 2 — Identify the jurisdiction.** Federal OSHA or an OSHA-approved State Plan; pull that jurisdiction's current adopted text of 1910.28 (and any State Plan amendments).
**Step 3 — Survey and measure.** Walk the site, list every walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge, and record the measured height to the lower level at each exposure point. Flag everything **>= 4 ft 0 in**.
**Step 4 — Select the means of protection** for each flagged exposure, from the three permitted categories: (A) guardrail system, (B) safety net system, or (C) personal fall protection system (personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning). Design each to the criteria in **1910.29** — e.g., guardrail systems with a top rail at **42 in (107 cm) +/- 3 in (8 cm)** and a midrail, and the specified strength/height criteria for nets and arrest systems.
**Step 5 — Check for a claimed exception** (Section 4 above). Each exception requires a documented feasibility determination, and where applicable the in-process-operation, limited-access, and 1910.30 training conditions. Absent that documentation, install conventional protection.
**Step 6 — Train.** Employees exposed to fall hazards must be trained per **1910.30** (nature of the hazards, correct procedures, and the fall protection systems in use) before exposure, with retraining when conditions or systems change.
**Step 7 — Verify and re-verify.** Re-measure after any change to the surface, the lower level, or the structure; a raised floor or a new pit can move an exposure from under 4 ft to 4 ft or more.

## 7. Related requirements that are not governed by the 4-foot side/edge trigger

Do not let the 4-foot answer mask obligations that attach differently:

- **Holes** — 1910.28(b)(3) protects employees from falling through holes (including skylights) that are **4 ft or more** above a lower level by covers, guardrails, travel restraint, or personal fall arrest; and separately protects employees from **tripping/stepping into or through holes less than 4 ft** above a lower level using covers or guardrails. Hole covers must meet 1910.29 and be marked/secured.
- **Guardrail/safety net/PFAS criteria** — 1910.29 sets the design, strength, and dimensional requirements for whatever system is chosen.
- **Training** — 1910.30.
- **General duty** — where a fall hazard exists below the 4-foot trigger and no specific standard covers it, OSHA Section 5(a)(1) can still apply to an unrecognized hazard; the 4-foot figure is a standard-specific trigger, not a safe harbor for all fall risk.

## 8. Bottom line for the record

> A US general-industry employer must protect an employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge from falling when the surface is **4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level**, by guardrail system, safety net system, or personal fall protection system — 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i). The 6-foot figure belongs to construction (29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1)) and does not apply here. Confirm the State Plan in force and document any claimed exception before departing from the 4-foot rule.

## 9. Assumptions and limits of this answer

- Assumes federal general industry (1910.28) is the applicable rule; assumes the current eCFR text governs, not an enforced-at-the-time prior version.
- Assumes an ordinary walking-working surface with no exception category applying; the answer is the general threshold, not a site-specific compliance determination.
- Whether a State Plan applies, and whether any exception in Section 4 is available at a particular site, are employer-specific determinations that must be made and documented on the facts; they do not change the 4-foot general-industry threshold stated here.
- Low-slope-roof subparagraph details in Section 4 item 4 should be verified against the current eCFR text before being written into a site procedure.

## 10. Sources

- 29 CFR 1910.28 (current), eCFR: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-XVII/part-1910/section-1910.28 — paragraphs (b)(1)(i), (b)(1)(ii), (b)(1)(iii), (b)(11)(i), (b)(12)(ii), (b)(13), (b)(14), (b)(15), and definitions (fetched 2026-11-17).
- OSHA standard page for 1910.28: https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.28
- Oregon OSHA Division 2, Subdivision D (State Plan text confirming the 4 ft (1.2 m) trigger and non-adoption of 1910.28(b)(1)(ii)): https://osha.oregon.gov/rules/final/division-2/pages/div2-subdivision-d.aspx

question: M6
answer:
ANSWER

A helicopter beginning a VFR flight in the United States must carry fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, in addition, reserve fuel sufficient to fly for at least 20 minutes at normal cruising speed / normal cruising fuel consumption after that point. The 20-minute figure applies day and night, and it is the same under Part 91 and Part 135 helicopter rules.

Legal answer: 20 minutes. It is expressed in the regulation as time, not volume; the fuel quantity that satisfies it is 20 minutes x the helicopter's normal-cruise fuel burn (see Section 4 for the conversion and worked examples).

1. REGULATORY BASIS (primary text)

14 CFR 91.151(b) — rotorcraft, VFR, Part 91:
'(b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.'

14 CFR 135.209(b) — helicopter, VFR, Part 135:
'(b) No person may begin a flight operation in a helicopter under VFR unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it has enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.'

FAA guidance, 'FAR Part 135 Helicopter VFR Operations' (faa.gov/media/32056, item 15): 'Reserve Fuel. FAR 135.209(b). During day or night the required reserve fuel is the amount that allows continued operation for 20 minutes.'

AC 194-1, Sec. 5.7.1: 'Section 135.209(b) states that helicopters must have enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, and to fly after that for at least 20 minutes regardless of day or nighttime.'

2. APPLICABILITY MATRIX — WHY THE ANSWER DOES NOT CHANGE WITH THE OPEN QUESTIONS

| Operating regime | Aircraft | Day VFR reserve | Night VFR reserve | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Part 91 | Rotorcraft (helicopter/gyroplane) | 20 min | 20 min | 91.151(b) |
| Part 135 | Helicopter | 20 min | 20 min | 135.209(b) |
| Part 91 | Airplane | 30 min | 45 min | 91.151(a) |
| Part 135 | Airplane | 30 min | 45 min | 135.209(a) |
| Part 91 | Helicopter, IFR | 30 min (not a VFR rule) | 30 min | 91.167(a)(3) |
| Part 135 | Helicopter, IFR | 30 min (not a VFR rule) | 30 min | 135.223(a)(3) |

Consequences for the flight in question:
- Day vs. night: irrelevant for a helicopter. Unlike airplanes, there is no 45-minute night reserve for rotorcraft under VFR. The 20 minutes is a floor at all hours.
- Part 91 vs. Part 135: irrelevant to the number. Both are 20 minutes. (Part 135 does add operational-control, ops-spec, and manual requirements that may impose more — see Section 6 — but the regulatory floor is identical.)
- The 30-minute helicopter figure that appears in 91.167(a)(3) and 135.223(a)(3) is the IFR reserve. It has no application to a VFR flight and must not be substituted for the 20-minute VFR figure.
- Powered-lift authorized for Copter procedures with vertical-lift landing capability may use the helicopter VFR minimum under 14 CFR 194.306(ss) (AC 194-1, Sec. 5.7.2). For an actual helicopter this is moot; the 20-minute rotorcraft figure governs directly.
- Part 121 helicopter VFR operations are vanishingly rare and outside the sources reviewed here; if a flight were ever conducted under Part 121, re-verify the applicable section before dispatch rather than assuming 20 minutes.

3. WHAT THE 20 MINUTES IS AND IS NOT

Is:
- A takeoff-time fuel state. The regulation is a condition on beginning the flight ('No person may begin a flight...'). The aircraft must be loaded with trip fuel plus 20 minutes of reserve before it lifts.
- Measured after the first point of intended landing. Reserve = fuel remaining overhead the first landing point, not fuel remaining at shutdown.
- Computed at normal cruising speed / normal cruising fuel consumption — i.e., the burn rate from the cruise portion of the AFM/POH performance data, adjusted for the planned cruise power setting, not best-range or max-endurance figures.

Is not:
- Alternate fuel. There is no VFR alternate-airport fuel requirement for a helicopter under Part 91 or Part 135; FAA guidance lists 'Alternate Fuel: N/A' for helicopter VFR.
- A substitute for the trip fuel calculation. The fuel to the first point of intended landing must be computed separately, considering wind and forecast weather (headwind component on the outbound leg, forecast temperatures, planned altitude).
- A landing margin you may plan to consume. You may not dispatch a flight whose planned landing fuel is zero by counting the reserve as usable trip fuel.
- A cap. It is a minimum. Operator manuals, ops specs, insurance policies, offshore/OCS rules, or pilot judgment routinely require more.

4. CONVERTING 20 MINUTES TO A FUEL QUANTITY

Formula (consistent units):
  Reserve (gal) = Normal-cruise burn rate (gal/hr) x (20 / 60) = Burn rate / 3
  Reserve (lb)  = Reserve (gal) x fuel density
  Reserve (kg)  = Reserve (lb) x 0.4536

Densities to use consistently: avgas 100LL = 6.0 lb/gal (0.72 kg/L); Jet A/A-1 = 6.7 lb/gal (0.80 kg/L). Use the POH/AFM value where it differs.

Worked examples (illustrative only — substitute your aircraft's actual AFM/POH cruise burn):

| Example | Normal-cruise burn | Reserve = burn / 3 | In pounds |
|---|---|---|---|
| Piston light helicopter, ~13 gal/hr 100LL | 13.0 gal/hr | 4.33 gal | 26.0 lb |
| Piston trainer, ~9 gal/hr 100LL | 9.0 gal/hr | 3.00 gal | 18.0 lb |
| Turbine single, ~33 gal/hr Jet A | 33.0 gal/hr | 11.0 gal | 73.7 lb |

Arithmetic check: 13.0 / 3 = 4.33; 9.0 / 3 = 3.00; 33.0 / 3 = 11.0. 4.33 x 6.0 = 25.98 (rounds to 26.0 lb); 3.00 x 6.0 = 18.0 lb; 11.0 x 6.7 = 73.7 lb.

Practical notes on the conversion:
- Use the burn rate for the planned cruise power setting and altitude, not the highest or lowest published figure. If the flight plan's cruise leg is at a reduced-power setting, use that leg's burn.
- Do not subtract unusable fuel from the reserve. Unusable fuel is outside the usable quantity; the 20 minutes must be usable fuel. Confirm the AFM unusable-fuel figure and verify by dipstick/totalizer rather than relying solely on float gauges.
- Wind does not change the fuel needed for 20 minutes of flight time (20 minutes of burn is 20 minutes of burn), but wind does change the trip fuel to the first landing point, and it changes where the aircraft is when the reserve clock starts. Plan the trip fuel with the forecast wind, then add the 20-minute reserve on top.
- Temperature/altitude affect fuel flow on turbine and normally-aspirated piston engines; use the performance chart for the forecast conditions.

5. COMPLIANCE PROCEDURE (preflight, repeatable)

Step 1. Compute trip fuel to the first point of intended landing: distance and time at planned cruise TAS, adjusted for forecast wind and temperature, plus taxi/startup/run-up/climb allowance from the POH.
Step 2. Compute reserve = 20 min x normal-cruise burn rate (Section 4).
Step 3. Sum: required fuel at brake release = trip fuel + reserve (+ any operator/ops-spec/insurance adders).
Step 4. Verify usable fuel on board by the most reliable means available (dipstick or totalizer cross-checked against gauges), not by gauge alone.
Step 5. Compare: usable on board must be >= required. If not, reduce payload or add fuel; do not reduce the reserve.
Step 6. Recompute if the forecast wind or the planned cruise altitude changes materially before departure.
Step 7. In flight, treat the reserve as a hard floor: if the fuel state at the first point of intended landing would be below 20 minutes, divert or land short. (This is airmanship and, for Part 135, an operational-control obligation; the regulation itself speaks to beginning the flight.)

Worksheet template:
  A. Trip time to first landing point ................ ______ hr
  B. Normal-cruise burn rate ......................... ______ gal/hr
  C. Trip fuel (A x B, plus taxi/climb allowance) .... ______ gal
  D. Reserve = B x 0.333 (20 min) .................... ______ gal
  E. Required at brake release (C + D + adders) ..... ______ gal
  F. Usable fuel on board (dipstick/totalizer) ...... ______ gal
  G. Margin (F - E) .................................. ______ gal  [must be >= 0]

6. REQUIREMENTS THAT CAN EXCEED 20 MINUTES

The 20-minute figure is a federal floor. Check, and comply with the highest applicable:
- Operator manuals and Part 135 ops specs / operations specifications fuel policies (e.g., helicopter air ambulance programs, offshore operators), which commonly require more.
- OCS/BSEE or other offshore regulations for over-water helicopter operations.
- Insurance policy terms and lease/owner minimums.
- 14 CFR 91.103 preflight action: the pilot must become familiar with all available information, including fuel requirements and alternatives — this supports, but does not numerically enlarge, the reserve.
- Prudent practice (non-regulatory): many operators add a contingency of roughly 10-20% of trip fuel or a fixed 10-15 minutes on top of the legal 20, and treat the legal reserve as untouchable. Labeled here as practice, not law.

7. COMMON ERRORS TO AVOID
- Applying the airplane 30/45-minute rule to a helicopter. Wrong aircraft category; the rotorcraft rule is a flat 20 minutes.
- Applying the 30-minute helicopter IFR reserve (91.167(a)(3), 135.223(a)(3)) to a VFR flight. Wrong rule set.
- Planning to land with the reserve already burned, i.e., using the 20 minutes as trip fuel.
- Using best-endurance or idle-descent burn rates instead of normal cruise.
- Ignoring unusable fuel or trusting fuel gauges alone.
- Forgetting that the reserve clock starts at the first point of intended landing, not at the destination after a planned en-route stop.

8. SOURCES
- 14 CFR 91.151 (eCFR, fetched 2026-11-17)
- 14 CFR 135.209 (eCFR, fetched 2026-11-17)
- 14 CFR Part 91 Subpart B, Part 135 Subpart D (eCFR, fetched 2026-11-17)
- FAA, fuel-requirements guidance document (faa.gov/media/32056), items 15 and 17
- FAA AC 194-1, Sec. 5.7 (powered-lift use of helicopter VFR fuel minimums)

BOTTOM LINE

20 minutes at normal cruising speed, day or night, Part 91 or Part 135 — measured after arrival at the first point of intended landing and carried in addition to the fuel needed to get there. Convert to volume as burn rate (gal/hr) divided by 3.

# Deprecation of TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1

## Answers

| Ask | Answer |
|---|---|
| 1. Which RFC deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1? | **RFC 8996**, *Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1* (March 2021; part of BCP 195). |
| 2. What status did it give the RFCs that had defined them? | **Historic** — RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0) and RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1) "have been moved to Historic status." |

## Detail

**The deprecating document.** RFC 8996, *Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1*, IETF Stream, published 23 March 2021, from `draft-ietf-tls-oldversions-deprecate-12`. Its own status is *Internet Best Current Practice* ("This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice"), and it is part of **BCP 195**, because it updates the TLS usage best-practice document RFC 7525. Do not conflate this with the answer to ask 2: BCP is RFC 8996's own status, not the status it conferred on the defining RFCs.

**Scope of the deprecation.** The abstract and Section 1 deprecate three protocol versions and move their defining documents to Historic:

| Protocol version | Defining RFC | Resulting status |
|---|---|---|
| TLS 1.0 | RFC 2246 | Historic |
| TLS 1.1 | RFC 4346 | Historic |
| DTLS 1.0 | RFC 4347 | Historic |
| DTLS 1.2 | RFC 6347 | **Not** deprecated (RFC 8996 updates RFC 6347 only to forbid negotiating DTLS 1.0) |

There is no DTLS 1.1. RFC 8996 also moves RFC 5469 (DES/IDEA cipher suites) to Historic, since the only TLS versions for which those suites were defined are now Historic.

**Precise mechanism (deprecate ≠ obsolete).** RFC 8996 does **not** obsolete RFC 2246 or RFC 4346. Both were already on the standards-track obsoletion chain: RFC 2246 was obsoleted by RFC 4346, and RFC 4346 by RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2); RFC 5246 was in turn obsoleted by RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3). What RFC 8996 adds is the formal deprecation of the protocol versions and the reassignment of the defining documents to the non-standards-track status **Historic**. The document also *updates* many RFCs that normatively reference TLS 1.0/1.1, plus RFC 7525 and RFC 6347.

**Stated rationale (Section 1).** The versions lack support for currently recommended cryptography — no AEAD cipher suites before TLS 1.2, handshake integrity and peer authentication both relying on SHA-1, and mandatory-to-implement legacy suites such as `TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA` in TLS 1.0 — and government/industry TLS profiles already mandate avoiding them. TLS 1.2 was the IETF-recommended version from 2008, giving ample transition time.

## Grounding

- RFC Editor info page and RFC HTML for RFC 8996 (abstract, Status of This Memo, Section 1): "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."
- IETF Datatracker document page for RFC 8996 (same abstract) and document history showing RFC 8996 dated 2021-03-23, replacing draft-ietf-tls-oldversions-deprecate-12.
- RFC 8996 inline errata page (same abstract and Section 1 text).
- Corroboration only (not load-bearing): NCSC *Using TLS to protect data* — "TLS 1.1 and 1.0 have also been deprecated by the IETF, as outlined in RFC 8996, and should not be used."

## Common pitfalls this answer avoids

1. **Confusing the two statuses.** RFC 8996's own status is Best Current Practice (BCP 195); the status it *assigned* is Historic. Only the latter answers ask 2.
2. **Saying RFC 8996 obsoletes RFC 2246/4346.** It does not; it deprecates the versions and moves the documents to Historic. Obsoletion came earlier via RFC 4346 → RFC 5246 → RFC 8446.
3. **Citing RFC 7525 or RFC 8446 as the deprecating document.** RFC 7525 is the earlier BCP 195 TLS-usage guidance that RFC 8996 updates; RFC 8446 defines TLS 1.3.
4. **Over-broad scope.** DTLS 1.2 is explicitly not deprecated.

question: M10
answer:
ANSWER

The US Social Security contribution and benefit base (the OASDI taxable maximum — the most wage and self-employment income subject to Social Security payroll tax) for tax year 2026 is $184,500.

Scope of that figure: it applies to the Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI) 6.2% employee / 6.2% employer / 12.4% self-employed tax, per worker, on 2026 calendar-year wages and self-employment income. Medicare's Hospital Insurance (HI) tax has had no earnings cap since 1993, so $184,500 is not a Medicare limit.

MAXIMUM TAX IMPLIED BY THE CAP (arithmetic cross-check)

- Employee share: 184,500 x 6.2% = $11,439.00
- Employer share: 184,500 x 6.2% = $11,439.00
- Combined employee + employer: $22,878.00
- Self-employed (both halves): 184,500 x 12.4% = $22,878.00

The $11,439.00 figure is corroborated independently: SSA Publication 42-007 (EFW2 Tax Year 2026, dated 11/12/2026) instructs filers that the Social Security Tax Withheld field 'should not exceed $11,439.00 for tax year 2026,' which is exactly 6.2% of $184,500.

SOURCES (all Social Security Administration, the statutorily designated authority)

1. SSA, Contribution and Benefit Base (https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html), table 'Contribution and benefit bases, 1937-2027': 2025 = $176,100; 2026 = $184,500; 2027 = $192,300.
2. SSA, Automatic Determinations in Recent Years (https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/autoAdj.html), 'Social Security program amounts determined under automatic adjustment provisions, 2017-2027': 2026 row shows COLA 3.6 percent, contribution and benefit base $184,500, retirement earnings test exempt amounts $24,480 (under normal retirement age) and $65,160 (year of attainment).
3. SSA Publication No. 42-007, EFW2 Tax Year 2026, Specifications for Filing Forms W-2 Electronically (https://www.ssa.gov/employer/efw/26efw2.pdf, dated 11/12/2026): 'The sum of this field and the Social Security Tips field should not exceed the annual maximum Social Security wage base for the tax year ($184,500 for tax year 2026).'
4. SSA, Contribution & Benefit Base — Calculation details (https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbbdet.html) and National Average Wage Index (https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/AWI.html), used below to re-derive the figure.

DERIVATION UNDER THE STATUTORY FORMULA (verification that $184,500 is the formula output, not just a transcription)

Statutory rule as stated by SSA: the base for any year Y after 1994 equals the 1994 base of $60,600 multiplied by the ratio of the national average wage index for year (Y-2) to that for 1992, rounded to the nearest multiple of $300, and never reduced below the current base. The formula applies only if a cost-of-living increase is effective for December of the year of determination.

For 2026 (Y = 2026, so Y-2 = 2024):
- 1994 base: $60,600
- 1992 average wage index: 22,935.42
- 2024 average wage index: 69,846.57
- Computation: 60,600 x 69,846.57 / 22,935.42 = $184,548.70
- Round to nearest multiple of $300: $184,548.70 is $48.70 below $184,500 and $251.30 below $184,800, so the result is $184,500.
- Not-reduced test: $184,500 exceeds the 2025 base of $176,100, so the reduction floor does not bind.

Result: $184,500, matching the published figure. Year-over-year increase: $184,500 - $176,100 = $8,400, or +4.77%.

The same page's 2027 determination confirms the chain and the 2026 value as its floor: 'the base for 2027 shall be the 1994 base of $60,600 multiplied by the ratio of the national average wage index for 2025 to that for 1992, or, if larger, the 2026 base of $184,500,' yielding $60,600 x 72,800.33 / 22,935.42 = $192,353.14, which rounds to $192,300. That the 2027 formula explicitly references 'the 2026 base of $184,500' is a further, independent confirmation of the 2026 figure.

STATUS OF THE FIGURE

The figure is final, not a projection or estimate. The SSA pages consulted were retrieved 2026-11-17 and already publish the 2027 determination (announced in the fall 2026 trustees/COLA cycle), which by construction takes the 2026 base as settled. The EFW2 specification for tax year 2026, published 11/12/2026, likewise hard-codes $184,500 as the reporting cap for that tax year.

COMMONLY CONFUSED ADJACENT VALUES (published at the same time; none of these is the payroll-tax cap)

- 2025 base: $176,100 — prior year, not 2026.
- 2027 base: $192,300 — following year, not 2026.
- 2026 COLA: 3.6 percent — benefit increase, not an earnings cap.
- 2026 retirement earnings test exempt amounts: $24,480 (beneficiaries under normal retirement age) and $65,160 (year of attainment) — these limit earnings of beneficiaries receiving benefits, not the tax base.
- 2026 'old-law' contribution and benefit base: $137,100 — a separate construct used for Railroad Retirement, ERISA and certain benefit-computation purposes; not the payroll-tax cap.
- 2026 earnings per quarter of coverage: $1,890.
- Medicare HI: no earnings cap; the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax applies above $200,000 single / $250,000 joint, which is an income-tax threshold, not part of FICA's taxable maximum.

CAVEATS A COMPLIANCE USER SHOULD NOTE

- The cap is per worker, per calendar year, and applies separately to wages and to self-employment income; an individual with both wage and self-employment income applies the single $184,500 limit across the combined total on the Form 1040 SE calculation (via the excess-Social-Security-wages credit), not twice.
- Multiple employers each withhold on wages up to the cap without coordination; over-withholding is recovered as a credit on the annual return.
- The figure is indexed annually to the national average wage index and will change for 2027 (to $192,300, already announced). Any 2026 answer must not be reused for a later tax year.

ANSWER

The limit on an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan for 2026, before any catch-up contribution, is $24,500.

This is the IRC §402(g)(1) limit on the exclusion for elective deferrals for the 2026 calendar year. It applies to pre-tax (traditional) elective deferrals and to designated Roth contributions alike — the $24,500 is a single combined ceiling, not $24,500 for each contribution type.

PRIMARY SOURCES

1. IRS Notice 2025-67 (2026 cost-of-living adjustments): "The limitation under section 402(g)(1) on the exclusion for elective deferrals described in section 402(g)(3), which includes elective deferrals made to the Thrift Savings Plan, is increased from $23,500 to $24,500."
2. IRS, Retirement Topics — 401(k) and Profit-Sharing Plan Contribution Limits: "The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments."
3. IRS, Retirement Topics — Contributions: "The basic limit on elective deferrals is $24,500 in 2026, $23,500 in 2025, $23,000 in 2024 and $22,500 in 2023, or 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less."
4. IRS Publication 560: "The basic limit on elective deferrals is $23,500 for 2025 and increases to $24,500 for 2026."

OPERATIVE DETAIL FOR APPLYING THE LIMIT

- Lesser-of rule. The statutory limit is the lesser of $24,500 or 100% of the employee's compensation. For any employee with compensation at or above $24,500, the dollar cap governs; below that, compensation governs.
- Aggregation across plans. The $24,500 is a per-individual, per-calendar-year limit, aggregated across all elective deferrals the individual makes to 401(k), 403(b), SARSEP, and SIMPLE plans (with the SIMPLE limit applying as a sub-cap of $17,000 for 2026), plus §457(b) deferrals where applicable. An employee with two employers or two 401(k) plans does not get $24,500 per plan; the employee is responsible for monitoring the combined total. Deferrals above the limit are includible in gross income; excess deferrals can be corrected by distribution (plus attributable earnings) if made by the statutory deadline (generally April 15 of the following year).
- Plan-level caps can be lower. A plan document may impose a lower deferral cap, and the plan must be administered in accordance with that lower cap. Highly compensated employees may also be limited below $24,500 by ADP nondiscrimination testing. The $24,500 is a statutory ceiling, not an entitlement.
- What the $24,500 does not include. Employer matching contributions, employer nonelective contributions, and forfeiture allocations are outside the §402(g) limit and are instead tested against the §415(c) annual additions limit of $72,000 for 2026 (excluding catch-up). Compensation that may be taken into account for plan purposes is capped at $360,000 for 2026.

CATCH-UP CONTEXT (EXCLUDED FROM THE $24,500, PROVIDED ONLY FOR BOUNDARY CLARITY)

- Age 50+ catch-up limit for 401(k)/403(b)/governmental 457(b)/TSP/SARSEP: $8,000 for 2026 (up from $7,500).
- Age 60–63 "super" catch-up (SECURE 2.0): $11,250 for 2026.
- Maximum deferral for a participant age 50–59 or 64+: $24,500 + $8,000 = $32,500. For a participant age 60–63 in 2026: $24,500 + $11,250 = $35,750.
- SECURE 2.0 Roth catch-up mandate: participants whose prior-year wages from the plan sponsor exceed the applicable threshold must make catch-up contributions on a Roth basis. The IRS Retirement Topics — Catch-Up Contributions page states this threshold as $150,000 for 2026, while Notice 2025-67 frames the same rule in terms of the 2025 wage threshold used to determine 2026 treatment. Because the two sources are worded differently on this point, the figure should be confirmed against Notice 2025-67's full text before being used in payroll configuration. This affects only catch-up contributions and therefore does not change the $24,500 answer.

SCOPE CONDITIONS (WHERE THIS ANSWER WOULD NOT APPLY)

- SIMPLE 401(k) plans: $17,000 for 2026, not $24,500.
- 403(b) plans with the 15-years-of-service rule: a participant may qualify for up to $27,500 for 2026; this provision does not exist for 401(k) plans and must not be applied to them.
- Section 457(b) governmental plans: $24,500 for 2026, with separate age-based and final-three-years increased limits; a separate plan type from the 401(k) asked about.
- Non-U.S. jurisdictions and nonqualified deferred compensation arrangements: outside the scope of this answer entirely.

RECOMMENDED PLAN COMMUNICATION

Payroll and the plan administrator should be configured to cap 2026 pre-tax plus Roth elective deferrals at $24,500 per participant, applying any lower plan-document cap or ADP-imposed HCE cap first, with catch-up contributions tracked in a separate bucket at $8,000 (or $11,250 for participants attaining age 60, 61, 62, or 63 in 2026). Participant notices should state the $24,500 figure, the 100%-of-compensation floor, the cross-plan aggregation rule, and the deadline for correcting excess deferrals.

| 2 | Primary 24-hour PM2.5 | **35 µg/m³** | 98th percentile 24-hour concentration, as determined under 40 CFR part 50, appendix N | 40 CFR 50.20(c) |

### Basis and date convention

- The governing final rule is EPA's **Reconsideration of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter**, signed February 7, 2024, published at **89 FR 16380 (Mar. 6, 2024)**, and codified at **40 CFR 50.20**.

40 CFR 50.18 remains in the CFR and contains the prior 2012 primary PM2.5 standards: **12.0 µg/m³** annual and **35 µg/m³** 24-hour. This answer reports **primary** standards only, as requested. Secondary (welfare-based) PM2.5 standards are not reported here. question: M4
answer:
ANSWER

In general industry (US federal OSHA, 29 CFR Part 1910), an employer must protect an employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge from falling when that surface is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level.

4 feet = 1.2 m (48 inches).

---

1. CONTROLLING STANDARD AND TEXT

Primary rule — 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i), 'Unprotected sides and edges':

  'Except as provided elsewhere in this section, the employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by one or more of the following: (A) Guardrail systems; (B) Safety net systems; or (C) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems.'

Parallel catch-all — 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(15), 'Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed' (confirmed verbatim in the fetched eCFR/govinfo text):

  'Except as provided elsewhere in this section or by other subparts of this part, the employer must ensure each employee on a walking-working surface 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by: (i) Guardrail systems; (ii) Safety net systems; or (iii) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems.'

Both provisions yield the same figure, so the answer is 4 ft (1.2 m) whether the surface is treated under the unprotected-side-and-edge paragraph or the residual paragraph.

---

2. KEY DEFINITIONS AFFECTING APPLICATION (29 CFR 1910.21(b))

- Walking-working surface: any horizontal or vertical surface on or through which an employee walks, works, or gains access to a work area or workplace location.
- Unprotected sides and edges: any side or edge of a walking-working surface (except at entrances and other points of access) where there is no wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system to protect an employee from falling to a lower level.
- Lower level: a surface or area to which an employee could fall (ground, floor, etc.).
- Hole: a gap or open space in a floor, roof, horizontal walking-working surface, or similar surface at least 2 in (5 cm) in its least dimension — holes have their own coverage requirements in 1910.28(b)(3)-(4) and are not answered by the 4 ft figure alone.

---

3. HOW TO MEASURE THE 4 FEET

Measure vertically from the walking-working surface on which the employee stands to the lower level to which the employee could fall. The duty attaches at 4 ft or more (i.e., at exactly 4 ft 0 in the trigger is met). Below 4 ft on an ordinary walking-working surface, 1910.28(b)(1) does not itself require a fall protection system; other duties still apply (see §7).

---

4. CARVE-OUTS AND OVERRIDES TO THE 4 FT TRIGGER (do not apply the 4 ft figure blindly)

The general rule in §1910.28(b)(1) is expressly subject to the rest of §1910.28. The following surface-specific provisions change the trigger or the required method; all are within general industry:

  Surface / condition                         Trigger / requirement
  ------------------------------------------  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  Ordinary walking-working surface with an    4 ft (1.2 m) or more -> guardrail, safety net, or personal fall
  unprotected side or edge; surfaces not     protection system. [1910.28(b)(1)(i); (b)(15)]
  otherwise addressed
  Dockboards                                  4 ft (1.2 m) or more -> guardrail system or handrails; exception
                                              where used solely for motorized materials handling, employees
                                              not exposed to falls >10 ft (3 m), and trained per 1910.30.
                                              [1910.28(b)(4)]
  Runways and similar walkways                4 ft (1.2 m) or more -> guardrail system; one side may be omitted
                                              if infeasible on a special-purpose runway, runway >=18 in (46 cm)
                                              wide, and PFAS/travel restraint used. [1910.28(b)(5)]
  Stairway landings                           4 ft (1.2 m) or more above a lower level -> guardrail or stair rail
                                              system. [1910.28(b)(11)(i)]
  Dangerous equipment                        Protection required regardless of height: employees less than 4 ft
                                              above dangerous equipment must be protected by guardrail or travel
                                              restraint (or the equipment covered/guarded); at 4 ft or more, the
                                              full system set applies. The 4 ft floor does not excuse protection.
                                              [1910.28(b)(6)]
  Low-slope roofs                            Trigger is distance from the roof edge, not height: work less than
                                              6 ft (1.6 m) from the edge requires guardrail, safety net, travel
                                              restraint, or PFAS; 6 ft to less than 15 ft (4.6 m) allows designated
                                              area/warning line alternatives; at 15 ft or more a work rule keeping
                                              employees 15 ft back may be used. [1910.28(b)(13)]
  Fixed ladders                              Ladders extending more than 24 ft (7.3 m) above a lower level have
                                              their own personal fall arrest / ladder safety system rules.
                                              [1910.28(b)(9)]
  Scaffolds and rope descent systems         Scaffolds: protect per 29 CFR Part 1926 Subpart L (referred out —
                                              not the 1910 4 ft figure). Rope descent systems: 4 ft (1.2 m) or
                                              more -> PFAS. [1910.28(b)(12)]
  Holes, pits, open pits                       Governed by their own cover/guardrail/attendant and marking rules;
                                              do not answer a hole question with the 4 ft figure alone.

If the employer can demonstrate that guardrail, safety net, or personal fall protection systems are infeasible or would create a greater hazard, §1910.28(b)(1)(ii) permits an alternative only through a written, implemented fall protection plan meeting §1910.29(k). Absent that documented demonstration, the 4 ft duty is met only by an actual system.

---

5. WHAT COUNTS AS PROTECTION AT 4 FT

Any one or more of:
  (a) Guardrail system — top rail 42 in (107 cm) +/- 3 in (8 cm) above the walking-working surface (top edge may exceed 45 in/114 cm if all other criteria are met), with midrail/screens/mesh/intermediate members or an equivalent 21 in (53 cm) wall/parapet, built and installed to §1910.29(b).
  (b) Safety net system — §1910.29(c).
  (c) Personal fall protection system — personal fall arrest (§1910.140), travel restraint, or positioning system, per §1910.29(d)-(f).

Toeboards/screens/guardrails, canopy structures, or barricades are additionally required where employees are exposed to falling objects (§1910.28(c)); those are falling-object duties, not substitutes for the fall protection itself.

---

6. ADJACENT DUTIES THAT TRAVEL WITH THE 4 FT ANSWER

- §1910.29: criteria and practices for the selected system (design, installation, inspection, maintenance).
- §1910.30: training is required before an employee uses fall protection equipment/systems or is exposed to fall hazards; retraining when the workplace or systems change or an employee shows inadequacy.
- §1910.28(a): the employer must select and install the systems this subpart requires, and comply with the other requirements of the subpart, before any employee begins work that necessitates fall or falling object protection.
- §1910.28(b)(1)(ii): documented fall protection plan where systems are infeasible or create greater hazard.

---

7. WHAT APPLIES BELOW 4 FEET

On an ordinary walking-working surface below 4 ft, §1910.28(b)(1) imposes no fall protection system duty. Protection obligations can still arise from: the dangerous-equipment provision (§1910.28(b)(6)) which has no height floor; hole/pit provisions; other subparts of Part 1910 (e.g., specific machinery or electrical rules); and the OSH Act general duty clause, §5(a)(1), for recognized hazards not covered by a specific standard.

---

8. JURISDICTION NOTE (state-plan states)

This answer states the federal general-industry figure. Roughly half the states and territories operate OSHA-approved state plans; state plans must be at least as effective as federal OSHA and may adopt a stricter (lower) trigger or additional requirements. The employer must confirm the controlling rule for the worksite's jurisdiction. Note that Oregon OSHA's own general-industry guidance confirms 4 ft as the general-industry trigger while flagging that some general-industry trigger heights differ (dangerous equipment at any height; scaffolds referred out) — the same structure described above.

---

9. CONSTRUCTION DISAMBIGUATION (excluded by the question, stated only to prevent confusion)

The 6 ft (1.8 m) trigger commonly quoted belongs to construction, 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1) (unprotected sides and edges, 6 ft or more above a lower level), and to certain other construction provisions. It is not the general-industry answer. Do not use 6 ft for Part 1910 general-industry walking-working surfaces; do not use 4 ft for Part 1926 construction.

---

10. COMPLIANCE STATEMENT / SIGNAGE-READY WORDING

'Fall protection is required when an employee is on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level. Required protection: guardrail system, safety net system, or personal fall protection system (29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i)). Exceptions for specific surfaces are listed in 29 CFR 1910.28(b); employees must be trained per 29 CFR 1910.30.'

---

11. CONSISTENCY VERIFICATION

- Answer figure stated: 4 ft (1.2 m, 48 in) — identical to the figure in both §1910.28(b)(1)(i) and §1910.28(b)(15) as quoted in the source passages.
- Every 4 ft figure used elsewhere in this summary (dockboards, runways, stairway landings, rope descent systems, dangerous-equipment full-system tier) is a 4 ft figure, so no example contradicts the general rule.
- The only non-4-ft numbers used (6 ft, 15 ft, 24 ft, 10 ft, 18 in, 21 in, 42 in) are each attributed to a specific carve-out provision and are not presented as the general trigger.
- No statement in this summary requires protection below 4 ft on an ordinary walking-working surface, and none treats 6 ft (the construction figure) as controlling in general industry.

# VFR reserve fuel for a helicopter — United States, Part 91 (and Part 135)

## Answer

**20 minutes of flight at normal cruising speed.** A helicopter may not begin a VFR flight in the US unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it carries enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing **and then fly for at least 20 more minutes at normal cruising speed**. This is the reserve beyond the fuel needed to reach the first point of intended landing.

The 20-minute figure is the same **day or night** — there is no night increase for rotorcraft.

## Governing regulation

14 CFR § 91.151, *Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions*:

> (a) No person may begin a flight in an airplane under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed—
> (1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or
> (2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes.
>
> **(b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.**

Paragraph (b) is the rotorcraft paragraph and it is the one that applies to a helicopter. Paragraph (a) — the 30-minute day / 45-minute night figures — applies to **airplanes** and must not be used for a helicopter. Note also that (b) contains no day/night split: 20 minutes is the minimum in both cases.

## What the 20 minutes means operationally

1. **It is a duration, not a quantity.** The regulation is written in minutes at normal cruising speed. A gallon or pound figure is derived, not regulatory.
2. **It is measured at normal cruising speed** — the speed the aircraft is expected to use in cruise, not hover, not max-range, not Vne.
3. **It is measured from the first point of intended landing**, i.e., it is fuel remaining *after* reaching that point, not fuel remaining at some intermediate waypoint.
4. **Wind and forecast weather must be considered** in computing the fuel to the first point of intended landing. A headwind forecast lengthens the en-route leg and therefore raises the total fuel required; it does not change the 20-minute reserve itself.
5. **It must be usable fuel.** Unusable fuel, fuel that cannot be delivered to the engine(s) in the expected attitude, and fuel that is not aboard at brake(s)-off/release do not count toward the reserve.
6. **No alternate airport is required for VFR**, so there is no statutory "destination-to-alternate" increment to add. The 20 minutes is the whole regulatory reserve increment.
7. **It is a floor, not a target.** 14 CFR § 91.103 (preflight action) independently requires the pilot in command to become familiar with all available information concerning the flight, including fuel requirements, and known delays (e.g., anticipated ATC holding, weather) must be provided for on top of the 20 minutes.

## Converting 20 minutes into a quantity (procedure)

Step 1 — Obtain the normal cruising fuel consumption from the FAA-approved rotorcraft flight manual (RFM/POH) performance section for the planned cruise power setting, altitude, and temperature. Use a burn rate that includes the planned mixture/engine setting; do not use a best-case book number.

Step 2 — Apply the conversion:

```
Reserve quantity = (normal cruise burn rate) x (20 / 60)
                 = (normal cruise burn rate) / 3
```

For a burn rate in gallons per hour, the reserve is in gallons; for pounds per hour, it is in pounds.

Step 3 — Add that quantity to the fuel computed to fly the planned route to the first point of intended landing (that leg computed with wind and forecast weather). The sum is the minimum fuel on board at start of flight.

Step 4 — Compare against the RFM/POH total usable capacity and any operator limit; if the sum exceeds usable capacity, the flight cannot legally be launched as planned and must be shortened, refueled en route, or replanned.

### Illustrative worked example (hypothetical burn rate — not an aircraft-specific figure)

Assume an RFM cruise fuel flow of 24 gal/hr (or, equivalently, 150 lb/hr) at the planned cruise power setting:

| Item | Computation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Reserve, gallons | 24 gal/hr × (20/60) hr = 24/3 | **8.0 gal** |
| Reserve, pounds | 150 lb/hr × (20/60) hr = 150/3 | **50 lb** |
| En-route fuel to first landing (example: 1.5 hr with wind) | 24 × 1.5 | 36.0 gal |
| Minimum fuel on board at start | 36.0 + 8.0 | **44.0 gal** |

Arithmetic check: 20 min = 0.333… hr; 24 × 0.333… = 8.0; 150 × 0.333… = 50. Both are exactly one-third of the hourly rate, consistent with the rule. The 8.0 gal / 50 lb figures are *examples keyed to an assumed burn rate*; the regulatory answer remains 20 minutes.

## Related figures, stated so they are not confused with the answer

| Situation | Rule | Reserve after first point of intended landing |
|---|---|---|
| **Helicopter, VFR, Part 91** | **§ 91.151(b)** | **20 min, day or night — the answer** |
| Helicopter, VFR, Part 135 (compensation or hire) | § 135.209(b) | 20 min, day or night — identical to Part 91 |
| Airplane, VFR, Part 91 | § 91.151(a) | 30 min day / 45 min night — **not applicable to helicopters** |
| Airplane, VFR, Part 135 | § 135.209(a) | 30 min day / 45 min night — not applicable |
| Helicopter, IFR, Part 91 | § 91.167(a)(3) | 45 min after the alternate (helicopters: 30 min) — IFR only, outside this question |

Note on powered-lift: under 14 CFR part 194 and FAA AC 194-1, a powered-lift that is assured of a safe landing in vertical-lift flight mode along the entire route may use the § 91.151(b) rotorcraft 20-minute VFR reserve; if it cannot, the airplane figures in § 91.151(a) apply. A conventional helicopter is unaffected — it uses (b).

## Common errors this answer guards against

- Applying the airplane 30-minute day / 45-minute night reserve to a helicopter. Wrong paragraph.
- Increasing the helicopter reserve at night. § 91.151(b) has no night provision; 20 minutes applies at night too.
- Quoting a fixed gallon figure (e.g., "10 gallons") as if it were regulatory. The rule is time-based; the quantity depends entirely on the individual aircraft's cruise fuel flow.
- Treating the 20 minutes as fuel to be burned en route. It must remain on board after the first point of intended landing.
- Forgetting that the en-route leg itself must be computed with wind and forecast weather; a strong headwind can make the *total* fuel requirement, not the reserve, the limiting factor.

## Bottom line

Minimum regulatory reserve for a helicopter beginning a VFR flight in the US: **20 minutes at normal cruising speed**, day or night, after the fuel needed to reach the first point of intended landing (14 CFR § 91.151(b)). Convert to gallons or pounds by dividing the RFM normal-cruise hourly fuel flow by three. Any higher figure imposed by an operator, client, or the pilot's own conservative planning is additional to, not a substitute for, this minimum.

# Answer

**1. The RFC that deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 is RFC 8996**, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1" (May 2021), which is part of BCP 195 (Best Current Practice) and whose memo status is "Internet Best Current Practice."

**2. RFC 8996 moved the RFCs that defined those versions to Historic status** — i.e. it reclassified them from Standards Track to **Historic**.

The two defining documents named explicitly in RFC 8996:

| TLS version | Defining RFC | Title | Status assigned by RFC 8996 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TLS 1.0 | **RFC 2246** | The TLS Protocol Version 1.0 (January 1999) | **Historic** |
| TLS 1.1 | **RFC 4346** | The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.1 (April 2006; obsoletes RFC 2246) | **Historic** |

So the short form of the answer is: **RFC 8996; status = Historie.**

## Evidence (verbatim, from the fetched RFC Editor pages)

RFC 8996, Abstract:

> "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been **moved to Historic status**. … This document also deprecates Datagram TLS (DTLS) version 1.0 (RFC 4347) but not DTLS version 1.2, and there is no DTLS version 1.1. … This document also updates the best practices for TLS usage in RFC 7568; hence, it is part of BCP 195."

RFC 8996, body (Section 1/2):

> "Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC 2246] and 1.1 [RFC 4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC 5246] in 2008, which has now itself been superseded by TLS 1.3 [RFC 8446]. … Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0. Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been **moved to Historic status**."

Corroboration on the receiving end — the RFC Editor index pages for the defining documents now show the reassigned status:

- RFC 2246 page: "RFC 2246: The TLS Protocol Version 1.0 … **Historic** … This RFC is now obsolete, see RFC 4346."
- RFC 4346 page: "RFC 4346: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.1 … **Historic** … This RFC is now obsolete, see RFC 5246."

## Precision notes (things that are easy to get wrong)

1. **"Historic" is the answer to ask 2; "Obsolete" is not.** Both RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 had *already* been obsoleted long before — 2246 by 4346 (2006), and 4346 by RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2, 2008). Obsolescence means "a newer specification supersedes this one"; Historic is the standarts-track disposition that says "this specification is no longer a candidate for the standards track and should not be used for new work." RFC 8996 is the document that performed the latter.
2. **Do not confuse RFC 8996's own status with the status it assigned.** RFC 8996 itself is an "Internet Best Current Practice" (BCP 195, updating RFC 7568). That is the status *of the deprecating memo*, not of the deprected protocol documents.
3. **Scope of the deprecation is broader than just TLS.** RFC 8996 also deprecates DTLS 1.0 (RFC 4347) — explicitly *not* DTLS 1.2, and it notes there is no DTLS 1.1 — and it moves RFC 5469 (DES/IDEA cipher suites for TLS) to Historic as a consequence. It also updates a long list of RFCs that normatively refer to TLS 1.0/1.1. None of that changes answers 1 and 2, but it should not be silently dropped in a compliance write-up.
4. **Nothing else deprecated these versions.** RFC 6176 (TLS 1.0/1.1 forbidding renegotiation), RFC 7567 (fallback SCSV), and RFC 7568 (BCP 195 best practices) all *restricted* TLS 1.0/1.1 usage but did not deprecate the protocol versions or reclassify the defining RFCs. RFC 8996 is the unique answer to ask 1.

## Citation block (ready to paste)

> Moriarty, K., Ed. and S. Farrell, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1", BCP 195, RFC 8996, DOI 10.17487/RFC 8996, May 2021. <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.html> (Abstract; Sections 1–2).
>
> Dierks, T. and C. Allen, "The TLS Protocol Version 1.0", RFC 2246, DOI 10.17487/RFC 2246, January 1999. <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2246> (status: Historie).
>
> Dierks, T. and E. Rescorla, "The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.1", RFC 4346, DOI 10.17487/RFC 4346, April 2006. <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4346> (status: Historie).

(Author lists and dates for RFC 8996 come from the RFC header block and were not part of the fetched excerpts; verify against the RFC's first page if the citation must be exact. The RFC numbers, the deprecation statement, and the Historic status assignment are all directly grounded in the fetched text.)

## Verification procedure (30 seconds, if you need to re-check)

1. Open <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.html>.
2. Read the Abstract: it names RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 and says they "have been moved to Historic status."
3. Read the header/"Status of This Memo": it says "Internet Best Current Practice" — confirming point 2 above.
4. Open <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2246> and <…/rfc4346>; both index pages render "Historic" in the status slot. Done.

## One-line answer

**RFC 8996 (BCP 195) deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 and moved their defining RFCs, RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0) and RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1), to Historic status.**

# 2026 US Social Security Contribution and Benefit Base

## Answer

**$184,500**

The contribution and benefit base (commonly the "taxable maximum") for calendar year 2026 is **$184,500** of earnings. This is the maximum amount of annual wages or self-employment income on which Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI) payroll tax is levied, and it is simultaneously the maximum annual earnings counted in an OASDI benefit computation.

- Applies to remuneration **paid in 2026** and to self-employment income earned in **tax years beginning in 2026**.
- Prior year (2025): $176,100. Increase: $8,400, or 4.77%.
- This is the official, finally determined figure — not a projection. It was announced 24 October 2025 and codified in the Federal Register on 3 November 2025 (90 FR 49047, doc. 2025-19763).

## Authority and corroboration

Four independent official statements agree:

1. **SSA press release, 24 Oct 2025** (ssa.gov/news/en/press/releases/2025-10-24.html): "the maximum amount of earnings subject to the Social Security tax (taxable maximum) is slated to increase to $184,500 from $176,100."
2. **SSA 2026 COLA Fact Sheet** (ssa.gov/news/en/cola/factsheets/2026.html), table "Maximum Taxable Earnings": Social Security (OASDI only) — 2025 $176,100; **2026 $184,500**. Same table: Medicare (HI only) — "No Limit."
3. **Federal Register, 3 Nov 2025, doc. 2025-19763** ("Automatic Increases to the Contribution and Benefit Base, Bend Points..."): "(1) The Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI) contribution and benefit base will be **$184,500** for remuneration paid in 2026 and self-employment income earned in tax years beginning in 2026."
4. **SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, Contribution and Benefit Base table** (ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html): 2026 = $184,500.

## Statutory derivation (section 230(b) of the Social Security Act)

The base for any year Y after 1994 equals the 1994 base of $60,600 multiplied by the ratio of the national average wage index for year (Y−2) to that for 1992, rounded to the nearest multiple of $300, and never reduced below the prior year's base. The formula applies only if a COLA becomes effective for December of the determination year; a 2.8% COLA applies for December 2025, so the formula is operative.

Inputs:
- 1994 base: $60,600
- 1992 national average wage index: $22,935.42
- 2024 national average wage index: $69,846.57

Computation:
1. Wage ratio: 69,846.57 ÷ 22,935.42 = 3.0453579...
2. 60,600 × 3.0453579 = **$184,548.71** (matches SSA's published intermediate figure exactly)
3. Round to nearest multiple of $300: 184,548.71 ÷ 300 = 615.1624 → 615 × 300 = **$184,500**
4. Floor test: $184,500 > $176,100 (2025 base), so the no-reduction rule does not apply and $184,500 is the base.

## What this means in tax terms (2026)

| Item | Rate | Base | Maximum OASDI tax |
|---|---|---|---|
| Employee | 6.2% | $184,500 | $11,439.00 |
| Employer (matching, per employee) | 6.2% | $184,500 | $11,439.00 |
| Self-employed (OASDI portion) | 12.4% | $184,500 | $22,878.00 |

- The base is **per worker, per year**, not per household. Each employer withholds and matches on that employer's own wages; there is no employer-side refund if an employee exceeds the cap across multiple employers.
- An employee who over-withholds because of multiple employers (or a mid-year employer change) recovers the excess as a credit on Form 1040 (Schedule 3, line 11) — the excess is not refunded by the employers.
- On Form W-2, this is the **Social Security wages** cap reported in Box 3 (Box 3 cannot exceed $184,500); Box 5 (Medicare wages) is uncapped.
- Elective deferrals to 401(k)/403(b)/457(b) plans **do not** reduce Social Security wages — they remain subject to OASDI up to the base. Cafeteria-plan (section 125) health premiums and qualifying commuter benefits *do* reduce OASDI wages.
- Self-employed individuals apply the same $184,500 base but deduct the employer-equivalent half of self-employment tax when computing income tax.

## Distinctions that are frequently confused with this figure (none of these is the answer)

- **Medicare (HI):** no taxable maximum in 2026. The 1.45% employee / 1.45% employer / 2.90% self-employed HI rates apply to all earnings.
- **Additional Medicare Tax:** 0.9% on earned income above $200,000 (single), $250,000 (MFJ), $125,000 (MFS). This is a surtax *threshold*, not a contribution base, and it is not indexed.
- **"Old-law" contribution and benefit base, 2026: $137,100.** Used only for Railroad Retirement tax/tier II, PBGC guarantee limits, special-minimum-benefit years of coverage, and certain non-covered-pension computations. It is *not* the payroll taxable maximum.
- **2027 base: $192,300** (computed from the 2025 wage index of $72,800.33). Wrong year — do not use for 2026.
- **Benefit-computation bend points for 2026:** $1,286 and $7,749 (PIA formula); maximum-family-benefit bend points $1,643 / $2,371 / $3,093. These are benefit formula parameters, not the contribution base.
- **Quarter of Coverage for 2026:** $1,890 of earnings.
- **COLA for 2026:** 2.8% (CPI-W, Q3 2024 → Q3 2025). The COLA drives benefits; the wage index drives the base. They are separate adjustments announced together.
- **Maximum Social Security benefit for a worker retiring at full retirement age in 2026:** $4,152/month. This is the "benefit" side of "contribution and benefit base" and is unrelated to the $184,500 earnings cap.

## One-line citable statement

> For 2026, the OASDI contribution and benefit base is $184,500 — the maximum amount of earnings subject to Social Security payroll tax (6.2% each for employee and employer; 12.4% for the self-employed), per SSA's 24 October 2025 announcement, its 2026 COLA Fact Sheet, and the Federal Register notice of 3 November 2025 (2025-19763).

ANSWER

2026 elective deferral limit (IRC §402(g)(1)), before any catch-up contribution: $24,500 per employee.

This is the officially announced figure, not a projection. The IRS released it in IR-2025-111 on November 13, 2025, and in the accompanying technical guidance, Notice 2025-67. It is an increase from $23,500 in 2025.

AUTHORITY

- Notice 2025-67: "The limitation under section 402(g)(1) on the exclusion for elective deferrals described in section 402(g)(3), which includes elective deferrals made to the Thrift Savings Plan, is increased from $23,500 to $24,500."
- IR-2025-111 (Nov. 13, 2025): "The annual contribution limit for employees who participate in 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457 plans, and the federal government's Thrift Savings Plan is increased to $24,500, up from $23,500 for 2025."
- IRS, Retirement topics — Contributions: "The basic limit on elective deferrals is $24,500 in 2026 ... or 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less."
- IRS, 401(k) and profit-sharing plan contribution limits: "The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments."
- IRS, COLA increases for dollar limitations: 401(k)/403(b)/profit-sharing elective deferrals, 2026 = 24,500.

HOW THE LIMIT OPERATES (what HR should apply)

1. Base limit: $24,500 for calendar year 2026, for a 401(k) plan (traditional, safe harbor, or with designated Roth features — Roth and pre-tax deferrals share this one limit).
2. Floor: capped at 100% of the employee's compensation if compensation is below $24,500.
3. Aggregation: the limit is per individual, not per plan. An employee who participates in more than one 401(k), 403(b), or governmental 457 plan (or the TSP) must aggregate elective deferrals across all of them against the single $24,500 figure. Excess deferrals are includible in gross income and must be corrected.
4. Timing: the limit is keyed to the calendar year in which the deferrals are made, regardless of the plan's fiscal year.
5. Catch-up is additive and excluded from the question: age 50+ catch-up is $8,000 for 2026 (ages 60–63: $11,250), and is not counted against the $24,500.
6. Plan-level limits can be lower: the plan document may cap deferrals below $24,500, and ADP/ACP nondiscrimination testing (or the §401(k)(3) limit) may further restrict highly compensated employees. Those are plan limits layered on top of, never above, the statutory figure.

RELATED 2026 FIGURES (for context; none of these is the answer)

- Age 50+ catch-up, 401(k): $8,000
- Ages 60–63 catch-up, 401(k): $11,250
- Overall §415(c) annual additions limit (deferrals + employer contributions, excluding catch-up): $72,000
- §401(a)(17) compensation cap: $360,000
- SIMPLE 401(k) elective deferral limit (different plan type, not the 401(k) answer): $17,000

SCOPE NOTE

This is the federal statutory limit under IRC §402(g) for a standard 401(k) plan for tax year 2026. It is not a state limit and not a plan-specific cap. If the intent was the total including catch-up, or the SIMPLE 401(k) figure, or the §415(c) overall limit, those are the separate numbers listed above.

answer:
CURRENT U.S. NATIONAL PRIMARY AMBIENT AIR QUALITY STANDARDS FOR PM2.5

ANSWER (primary, health-based standards, as codified at 40 CFR § 50.20):
  • Annual level: 9.0 µg/m³ — annual arithmetic mean concentration
  • 24-hour level: 35 µg/m³ — 24-hour average concentration (98th percentile form)

Both are expressed in micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³) of PM2.5, defined in the regulation as particles with an aerodynamic diameter less than or equal to a nominal 2.5 micrometers.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. AUTHORITATIVE TEXT (operative section, 40 CFR § 50.20)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

§ 50.20 National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5.

  "(a) The national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration measured in the ambient air as PM2.5 (particles with an aerodynamic diameter less than or equal to a nominal 2.5 micrometers) by either: (1) A reference method based on appendix L to this part and designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter; or (2) An equivalent method designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter.

   (b) The primary annual PM2.5 standard is met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N to this part, is less than or equal to 9.0 µg/m3.

   (c) The primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard is met when the 98th percentile 24-hour concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N to this part, is less than or equal to 35 µg/m3."

  Source citation as printed: [89 FR 16380, Mar. 6, 2024]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. STANDARD-BY-STANDARD TABLE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

| Averaging time | Level      | Form of the standard (how compliance is judged)                                             | Data handling  | Citation / rule           | Effective      |
|----------------|------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------|---------------------------|----------------|
| Annual         | 9.0 µg/m³  | Annual arithmetic mean, 3-year average of annual arithmetic means, ≤ 9.0 µg/m³                | 40 CFR pt. 50, app. N | § 50.20(a),(b); 89 FR 16380 (Mar. 6, 2024) | May 2024 (60 days after publication) |
| 24-hour        | 35 µg/m³   | 98th percentile of 24-hour concentrations, 3-year average of annual 98th percentiles, ≤ 35 µg/m³ | 40 CFR pt. 50, app. N | § 50.20(a),(c); 89 FR 16380 (Mar. 6, 2024) | May 2024 (60 days after publication); level unchanged from the 2012 review (78 FR 3277) |

Reference/equivalent method basis for both: appendix L reference method or an equivalent method designated under 40 CFR part 53.

Rounding conventions used in the comparison (per appendix N): annual arithmetic means are rounded to the nearest 0.1 µg/m³ before comparison to 9.0 µg/m³; 24-hour values are rounded to the nearest 1 µg/m³ before percentile computation and comparison to 35 µg/m³. A year of data is usable only if each calendar quarter meets the appendix N completeness requirement (nominally 75% data capture of scheduled sampling days), and the standard is evaluated on a 3-year average.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. RECONCILIATION OF THE 12.0 µg/m³ FIGURE — DO NOT REPORT IT AS CURRENT
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The source set contains two PM2.5 primary-standard sections, and they disagree on the annual level:

  • 40 CFR § 50.18 (text carrying [78 FR 3277, Jan. 15, 2013]): "...12.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration..." — with § 50.18(b) and (c) phrased identically to § 50.20(b) and (c) but with 12.0 µg/m³.
  • 40 CFR § 50.20 (text carrying [89 FR 16380, Mar. 6, 2024]): "...9.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration..."

The 2025 edition table of contents for 40 CFR part 50 lists both "50.18 National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5" and "50.20 National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5," confirming that § 50.18 was left standing in the Code as the pre-2024 text while the 2024 reconsideration was codified in a new section. § 50.20 is the later codification (2024 vs. 2013) and is therefore the operative current primary standard; § 50.18 carries the superseded 12.0 µg/m³ annual level. Where the two conflict, the later rule controls.

Practical consequence: an analyst who reads only § 50.18 will report 12.0 µg/m³ and be wrong about the current standard. The 24-hour level is unaffected by this conflict — it is 35 µg/m³ under both sections and has been 35 µg/m³ since the 2012 review.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. CURRENCY VERIFICATION PROCEDURE (how to confirm before publication/use)
