question: M4
answer:
ANSWER

In general industry (not construction), a US employer must protect an employee who is on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level. The trigger height is 4 feet.

PRIMARY CITATION

29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i):

  'Except as provided elsewhere in this section, the employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by one or more of the following: (A) Guardrail systems; (B) Safety net systems; or (C) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems.'

This is the current federal rule, in force since the Walking-Working Surfaces final rule (81 FR 82494) took effect on January 17, 2017.

DEFINITIONS THAT BOUND THE ANSWER (29 CFR 1910.21(b))

- Walking-working surface: any horizontal or vertical surface on or through which an employee walks, works, or gains access to a work area or workplace location.
- Unprotected sides and edges: any side or edge of a walking-working surface (except at entrances and other points of access) where there is no wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system to protect an employee from falling to a lower level.

So the duty attaches when both conditions hold: (a) a walking-working surface, and (b) a side or edge of it that lacks a wall, guardrail, or stair rail, with a drop of 4 ft or more to the lower level. A wall, guardrail, or stair rail at the edge removes the edge from 'unprotected' and the 4-foot duty is satisfied by that barrier.

MEASUREMENT

'4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level' is measured from the walking-working surface on which the employee stands to the lower level below. Exactly 4 ft is inside the duty ('4 feet or more'); 3 ft 11 in is outside it.

SCOPE AND EXCLUSIONS

1. Industry. This is the general-industry rule, 29 CFR Part 1910, Subpart D. Construction work governed by 29 CFR Part 1926 uses a different trigger — 6 feet (29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1)) — and is expressly out of scope here.
2. Superseded figure. The pre-2017 general-industry rule, former 29 CFR 1910.23(c)(1), used 5 feet. That figure is obsolete; any document still citing 5 ft for general industry is citing the pre-2017 standard. Answer 4 ft for current federal OSHA.
3. Jurisdiction. The 4-foot figure is the federal OSHA floor. OSHA-approved State Plans must be at least as effective as federal OSHA and may adopt a stricter (lower) threshold or additional requirements; the employer must check the State Plan standard that actually governs the workplace. (Oregon OSHA, for example, adopts 1910.28(b)(1)(i) at 4 ft verbatim, with state-specific additions.)
4. 'Except as provided elsewhere in this section.' The 4-foot general trigger yields to more specific provisions in 1910.28. None of those specific provisions sets a general height threshold below 4 ft for an unprotected edge; they either restate 4 ft for a particular surface or use distance-from-edge criteria for roofs. The employer must apply the specific provision where one exists.

SPECIFIC PROVISIONS THAT RESTATE OR MODIFY THE TRIGGER (for completeness; all consistent with the 4 ft general answer)

- Stairway landings, unprotected side or edge: 4 ft (1910.28(b)(11)(i)).
- Rope descent systems: 4 ft (1910.28(b)(12)(ii)).
- Slaughtering facility platforms, unprotected working side: 4 ft (1910.28(b)(14)(i)).
- Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed: 4 ft (1910.28(b)(15)).
- Low-slope roofs: keyed to distance from the roof edge, not height above a lower level — within 6 ft of the edge, full fall protection (1910.28(b)(13)(i)); 6 ft to 15 ft from the edge, full protection or a designated area for infrequent and temporary work (b)(13)(ii); 15 ft or more from the edge, no fall protection required if the work is infrequent and temporary, plus an enforced work rule (b)(13)(iii).
- Fixed ladders: 1910.28(b)(9) imposes ladder safety system / personal fall arrest requirements keyed to ladder height and installation date, not to the 4 ft edge trigger.
- Holes, hoist areas, ramps, and other enumerated surfaces each carry their own 1910.28(b) provision; where an employee is exposed to a 4 ft or greater drop at an unprotected edge and no more specific provision applies, (b)(1)(i) or the catch-all (b)(15) governs.

WHAT SATISFIES THE DUTY

One or more of: guardrail system, safety net system, or personal fall protection system (personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning system), each meeting the criteria and practices in 29 CFR 1910.29. Where guardrail, net, or personal fall protection is demonstrably infeasible or creates a greater hazard on residential roofs, a written fall protection plan meeting 29 CFR 1926.502(k) plus training meeting 1926.503(a) and (c) is required (1910.28(b)(1)(ii)).

ASSOCIATED DUTIES TRIGGERED WITH THE HEIGHT THRESHOLD

Identifying and evaluating fall hazards; selecting and installing compliant systems (1910.29); training employees who use fall protection and who are exposed to fall hazards (1910.30); and re-training when workplace changes or employee performance shows the need.

ONE-LINE ANSWER FOR A POLICY OR SIGN

'Employees on a walking-working surface 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level, at an unprotected side or edge, must be protected from falling by a guardrail system, safety net system, or personal fall protection system.'

REFERENCES

- 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) (eCFR current; GovInfo CFR 2024 title 29 vol 5).
- 29 CFR 1910.21(b) (definitions of walking-working surface; unprotected sides and edges).
- 29 CFR 1910.29, 1910.30 (criteria/practices; training).
- 81 FR 82494 (Walking-Working Surfaces and Personal Fall Protection Systems final rule; effective January 17, 2017).
- 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1) (construction, 6 ft — excluded by scope).

question: M6
answer:
HELICOPTER VFR RESERVE FUEL — US REGULATORY MINIMUM

ANSWER
A helicopter must carry fuel for 20 minutes of flight, at normal cruising speed, beyond the fuel needed to fly to the first point of intended landing, before beginning a VFR flight in the United States. The 20-minute figure applies both day and night; there is no day/night split for rotorcraft. This is a time requirement, not a gallon requirement — the corresponding fuel quantity is 20 minutes times the helicopter's normal-cruise fuel consumption.

1. CONTROLLING REGULATION (Part 91, general operating rules)
14 CFR 91.151(b), verbatim: "No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

Note the contrast with 91.151(a) for airplanes — 30 minutes day, 45 minutes night. Those figures do not apply to rotorcraft. A helicopter flying at night under VFR still owes 20 minutes, not 45.

2. COMMERCIAL OPERATIONS (Part 135)
14 CFR 135.209(b), verbatim: "No person may begin a flight operation in a helicopter under VFR unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it has enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."
Same 20 minutes, expressed as fuel consumption rather than speed. So the answer is 20 minutes whether the flight is flown under Part 91 or Part 135.

3. WHAT THE 20 MINUTES IS AND IS NOT
- It is in addition to trip fuel to the first point of intended landing. It is not a portion of trip fuel and cannot be counted twice.
- It is computed at normal cruising speed / normal cruising fuel consumption — i.e., use the cruise fuel flow from the flight manual or the operator's approved performance data at the planned cruise power setting, not climb, hover, or approach fuel flow.
- Wind and forecast weather must be considered in establishing the trip fuel to the first point of intended landing. A tailwind cannot be assumed for the reserve itself; the regulation states the reserve as time at normal cruising speed, so compute it at the normal-cruise burn for the type.
- It is a minimum, not a target. Operator policy, a Part 135 certificate holder's fuel policy, the aircraft flight manual, and prudent fuel planning for the actual conditions may require more. The regulation sets a floor only.
- No alternate-airport reserve is required for VFR; that is an IFR concept (91.167(a)(2)-(3), which for helicopters requires 30 minutes after the alternate, or after the destination when no alternate is required). Do not import the IFR 30-minute helicopter figure into a VFR plan.
- Fuel below the reserve must remain usable in flight — i.e., the reserve must be in usable fuel, not trapped or unusable quantity.

4. CONVERSION FROM TIME TO FUEL QUANTITY
Required reserve fuel (gal or lb) = (20 / 60) x normal-cruise fuel flow = 0.3333 x cruise fuel flow

Procedure:
Step 1. From the flight manual / operator performance data, take the fuel flow at the normal cruise power setting planned for the flight (gal/hr or lb/hr). Use the same units as the aircraft's usable-fuel indication.
Step 2. Multiply by 0.3333 (one third of an hour).
Step 3. Add that quantity to the trip fuel computed to the first point of intended landing, considering wind and forecast weather.
Step 4. Compare total required fuel to usable fuel on board. If usable fuel on board is less than trip fuel plus reserve, the flight may not begin.
Step 5. Confirm the result also satisfies any higher operator, certificate, or flight-manual minimum.

Worked example (illustrative numbers only — substitute the actual type's data):
- Normal cruise fuel flow: 16 gal/hr
- Trip fuel to first point of intended landing, wind and forecast considered: 1.5 hr x 16 = 24 gal
- Reserve: 0.3333 x 16 = 5.3 gal (20 minutes)
- Minimum usable fuel at start: 24 + 5.3 = 29.3 gal
- Second illustration: at 12 gal/hr cruise, the reserve is 4.0 gal; at 30 gal/hr, it is 10.0 gal. The time is fixed at 20 minutes; only the quantity scales.

5. COMMON ERRORS TO AVOID
- Applying the airplane 30/45-minute day/night figures to a helicopter.
- Applying the IFR helicopter 30-minute figure (91.167(a)(3)) to a VFR flight.
- Computing the reserve at climb or hover fuel flow instead of normal cruise.
- Treating the 20 minutes as included in the trip fuel rather than additive.
- Planning to arrive at the first landing point with exactly the reserve and no margin for wind or weather change — the rule requires the fuel to exist at the start of the flight considering wind and forecast weather, and practical planning normally adds margin above the legal floor.

6. VERIFICATION NOTE
The quoted text is the current eCFR and GovInfo CFR text for 14 CFR 91.151 and 135.209. Fuel regulations are subject to amendment; confirm the current text of 91.151(b) (and 135.209(b) if operating commercially) at the time of use. The answer above — 20 minutes, day or night, additive to trip fuel, at normal cruising speed — is the regulatory minimum.

## Answer

**1. Deprecating RFC: RFC 8996** — "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1" (March 2021), part of BCP 195, status "Internet Best Current Practice".

**2. Status given to the defining RFCs: Historic.** RFC 8996 moved the documents that defined TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 to **Historic** status. Specifically:

| Protocol | Defining RFC | Title | Original category | Status assigned by RFC 8996 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TLS 1.0 | **RFC 2246** | The TLS Protocol Version 1.0 (January 1999) | Standards Track | Historic |
| TLS 1.1 | **RFC 4346** | The TLS Protocol Version 1.1 (April 2006) | Standards Track | Historic |

### Primary-source support

RFC 8996, Abstract (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.html):

> "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."

RFC 8996, Section 1 (Introduction):

> "Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1 [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008... Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0. Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to Historic status."

Defining-RFC identification confirmed from the documents' own title blocks: RFC 2246 is "The TLS Protocol Version 1.0" (Dierks & Allen, January 1999) and RFC 4346 is "The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.1" (Dierks & Rescorla, April 2006), which itself carries "Obsoletes: 2246".

### Two status notions that must not be conflated

- **Historic** is the *status* (the maturity level in the RFC Editor / IANA metadata) that RFC 8996 assigns to RFC 2246 and RFC 4346. This is the answer to the question as asked.
- **Obsolete / "Obsoleted by"** is a *relationship* recorded in the RFC index, not the status field. RFC 2246 was already obsoleted by RFC 4346 in 2006; RFC 8996 now obsoletes both. In the RFC Editor index, RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 therefore show both "Obsoleted by: RFC 8996" and "Status: Historic". If the requester's tooling reads the "Obsoletes" header rather than the status field, the answer is expressed as "RFC 8996 obsoletes RFC 2246 and RFC 4346"; either way the *status* conferred is Historic.

### Scope notes

- RFC 8996 also deprecates **DTLS 1.0 (RFC 4347)** and moves it to Historic; it does **not** deprecate DTLS 1.2, and there is no DTLS 1.1.
- RFC 8996 additionally updates many RFCs that normatively reference TLS 1.0/1.1 (and RFC 7525), and it moves RFC 5469 to Historic. Those are collateral updates, not the status of the defining RFCs.
- "Deprecated" here is an IETF standards-track statement, not a vendor or regulatory mandate. Bodies such as NCSC independently state that TLS 1.0 and 1.1 "have been deprecated by the IETF, as outlined in RFC 8996" — consistent, but secondary.

### One-line citation form

EMPLOYEE ELECTIVE DEFERRAL LIMIT — 401(k) PLAN, TAX YEAR 2026 (BEFORE CATCH-UP)

ANSWER
  $24,500
  The maximum an employee may elect to defer into a 401(k) plan for 2026 under IRC §402(g)(1), before any catch-up contribution. Up from $23,500 for 2025. Effective for taxable years beginning January 1, 2026.

AUTHORITY (three independent IRS artifacts, all agreeing)
  1. IRS Notice 2025-67 (the annual COLA notice for 2026), §402(g) paragraph: "The limitation under section 402(g)(1) on the exclusion for elective deferrals described in section 402(g)(3) ... is increased from $23,500 to $24,500."
  2. IRS News Release IR-2025-111, dated November 13, 2025: "The annual contribution limit for employees who participate in 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457 plans, and the federal government's Thrift Savings Plan is increased to $24,500, up from $23,500 for 2025."
  3. IRS Retirement Topics — 401(k) and Profit-Sharing Plan Contribution Limits: "The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments."
  Also confirmed at IRS Retirement Topics — Contributions: "The basic limit on elective deferrals is $24,500 in 2026 ... or 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less."

SCOPE AND APPLICATION RULES (state these wherever the number is published internally)
  a. What counts against the $24,500: pre-tax (traditional) elective deferrals and designated Roth elective deferrals combined. They share one §402(g) limit; electing Roth does not create extra room.
  b. Aggregation: the limit is per person, not per plan. An employee must aggregate elective deferrals across all 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457(b) and TSP plans in which they participate. Excess deferrals must be corrected (distribution of excess plus attributable earnings by the applicable deadline).
  c. Compensation floor: the operative cap is the lesser of $24,500 or 100% of the employee's compensation. Low-pay, partial-year, and newly eligible employees can therefore have a lower effective cap.
  d. Plan-imposed limits: the plan document may set a lower deferral cap, and nondiscrimination testing (ADP) may force a lower cap on highly compensated employees. $24,500 is a statutory ceiling, not a promise of plan-level availability.
  e. Catch-up is excluded from this figure by design — see the table below. Do not add catch-up into the base limit when configuring payroll.
  f. Employer contributions (match, nonelective, forfeitures) do not count against §402(g); they count against §415(c) ($72,000 for 2026). Employee after-tax (non-Roth) contributions also do not count against §402(g).

2026 CROSS-REFERENCE TABLE (all 2026; keeps the base limit distinct from adjacent figures)
  §402(g) elective deferral limit, 401(k)/403(b)/gov. 457(b)/TSP ... $24,500  <-- THE ANSWER
  Age 50+ catch-up, same plans (additive, not included above) ..... $8,000
  Age 60-63 enhanced catch-up, same plans (in lieu of $8,000) ..... $11,250
  Maximum for an age 50-59 participant (24,500 + 8,000) ............ $32,500
  Maximum for an age 60-63 participant (24,500 + 11,250) ........... $35,750
  §415(c)(1)(A) annual additions cap (all sources) ................. $72,000
  §401(a)(17) compensation limit used for contributions ............ $360,000
  SIMPLE 401(k) elective deferral limit (different plan type) ....... $17,000
  SIMPLE catch-up age 50+ / age 60-63 ............................. $4,000 / $5,250
  Starter 401(k) deferral-only arrangement ........................ $6,000

VERIFICATION PERFORMED
  - $24,500 does not exceed the §415(c)(1)(A) annual-additions cap of $72,000 for the same year. Consistent.
  - $24,500 is the figure for tax year 2026 only. Notice 2026-66 sets the 2027 §402(g) limit at $25,500 (with a $8,500 age-50 catch-up). Do not use $25,500 for 2026; it appeared in the source set solely as the following-year figure.
  - $24,500 matches the §457(e)(15) limit for governmental 457(b) plans for 2026, which is correct and expected (the two have moved together), but they are separate limits applied to separate plan types.
  - SIMPLE 401(k) at $17,000 is not an alternative answer to this question; it applies only to SIMPLE 401(k) arrangements.

PAYROLL IMPLEMENTATION NOTE
  Set the annual pre-tax + Roth deferral election cap at $24,500 for 2026 (pro-rated per pay period as the plan provides). Do not suppress the cap for participants age 50+; instead allow the additional $8,000 (or $11,250 for those attaining 60-63 in 2026) as a separately coded catch-up bucket. Note the 2026 Roth catch-up requirement: participants whose prior-year FICA wages from the sponsor exceeded $150,000 must make catch-up contributions on a Roth basis if the plan offers Roth.

CAVEAT
  Figures are the federal statutory limits per IRS Notice 2025-67 and IR-2025-111. State or local rules do not alter them, but a plan's own document, collective bargaining agreement, or nondiscrimination testing may reduce the amount an individual may actually defer. Confirm against the plan document before communicating an individual's maximum.

# Current US National Primary Ambient Air Quality Standards for PM2.5

## 1. Answer

| Standard | Level | Form (how compliance is determined) | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Primary annual PM2.5** (health-based) | **9.0 µg/m³** | Annual arithmetic mean concentration, averaged over 3 consecutive years, less than or equal to 9.0 µg/m³ | 40 CFR 50.20 (promulgated 89 FR 16202, Feb. 7, 2024; effective May 6, 2024) |
| **Primary 24-hour PM2.5** (health-based) | **35 µg/m³** | 98th percentile of 24-hour concentrations, averaged over 3 consecutive years, less than or equal to 35 µg/m³ | 40 CFR 50.13(c) (71 FR 61224, Oct. 17, 2006, as amended 81 FR 58149, Aug. 24, 2016); retained unchanged by the 2024 rule |

Units throughout: micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³) of PM2.5, measured in ambient air as particles with an aerodynamic diameter ≤ 2.5 µm, by an FRM based on 40 CFR Part 50 Appendix L or an FEM designated under 40 CFR Part 53.

**Short form: annual = 9.0 µg/m³; 24-hour = 35 µg/m³.**

## 2. Why these numbers and not the others in Part 50

Part 50 currently contains several PM2.5 sections because EPA has revised the standards repeatedly and left the older text in place for residual purposes. Reading the wrong section is the standard failure mode here, so the full map is given below.

| CFR section | What it is | Annual level | 24-hour level | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 50.7 | 1997 PM2.5 NAAQS | 15.0 | 65 | **Superseded.** The 24-hour 65 µg/m³ was replaced in 2006; do not use. |
| 50.13 | 2006 24-hour NAAQS + retained 1997 annual/secondary text | 15.0 (1997 annual — not the current primary annual) | **35 (current primary and secondary 24-hour)** | Annual figure here is superseded for primary purposes per 50.13(d); 24-hour figure is operative. |
| 50.18 | 2012 primary annual NAAQS | 12.0 | — | **Superseded** by the 2024 reconsideration. |
| 50.20 | 2024 primary annual NAAQS | **9.0** | — | **Current primary annual standard.** |
| 50.13(a) (secondary clause) | Secondary annual (welfare-based) | 15.0 | 35 | Current but *secondary* — outside the scope of this request, listed only to explain the 15.0 that appears in 50.13. |

Two traps this table resolves explicitly:

1. **15.0 µg/m³ is not the current primary annual standard.** It is the 1997 annual value, now the *secondary* annual standard and, per 50.13(d), still applicable only to areas designated nonattainment for the 1997 primary annual NAAQS until redesignation to attainment. It does not describe the current primary annual standard.
2. **65 µg/m³ is revoked.** It is the 1997 24-hour level from 50.7 and must not be reported as current. The operative 24-hour level is 35 µg/m³.

## 3. Provenance and date of applicability

- **Annual:** EPA's PM NAAQS rule summary states: "On February 7, 2024, EPA strengthened the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter (PM NAAQS)... EPA is setting the level of the primary (health-based) annual PM2.5 standard at 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter." Codified at 40 CFR 50.20 ("National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5"), which appears in the Part 50 table of contents alongside 50.13 and 50.18.
- **24-hour:** Same EPA page: "EPA is not changing the current: primary and secondary (welfare-based) 24-hour PM2.5 standards..." The unchanged 24-hour level is confirmed by the codified text of 40 CFR 50.13(a) and (c) (35 µg/m³, 98th percentile form), and identically by the 2024 print of 40 CFR Part 50.
- **As-of date:** the underlying sources were retrieved 2026-11-17; the codified levels as of that retrieval are 9.0 and 35 µg/m³.

## 4. Currency caveat and verification step

EPA's PM NAAQS page carries a March 12, 2025 announcement of a "path forward" / reconsideration of the PM2.5 NAAQS. No final rule changing the codified levels appears in the available record, so the operative standards remain **9.0 µg/m³ annual** and **35 µg/m³ 24-hour**. Before relying on this in a regulatory filing or a compliance deadline calculation, run this one check:

1. Open 40 CFR 50.20 and 40 CFR 50.13 on eCFR (ecfr.gov/current/title-40/part-50) and read the current numeric levels in subsections (a)–(c). If 50.20 still reads 9.0 and 50.13(c) still reads 35, this answer stands.
2. Check the Federal Register for any final rule titled "Reconsideration of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter" published after Feb. 7, 2024. A final rule that revises the annual level supersedes the 9.0 figure in this answer; a rule that retains it does not.
3. Note that a change to a standard's *level* is distinct from a change to its *designations*; new nonattainment designations do not alter the numeric level.

- "Current" = the standards in force as of the source retrieval date (2026-11-17), i.e., the operative codified standards, not a pending proposal.
- "Level" = the numeric concentration limit. The form/statistical interpretation is supplied above because the annual and 24-hour standards are not comparable without it (an annual mean versus a 98th-percentile 24-hour value).
- Primary (health-based) standards only, as requested. The secondary annual standard (15.0 µg/m³) and secondary 24-hour standard (35 µg/m³) are noted only where needed to avoid version confusion.
- Units are µg/m³, the conventional and codified convention for PM2.5.

answer:

In general industry (US federal OSHA, 29 CFR Part 1910), the trigger height is 4 feet (1.2 m).

29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) — Unprotected sides and edges:

"Except as provided elsewhere in this section, the employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by one or more of the following: (A) Guardrail systems; (B) Safety net systems; or (C) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems."

The same 4-foot trigger is restated in the catch-all provision, 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(15) ("Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed"): each employee on a walking-working surface 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level must be protected by guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall protection systems.

So: at 4 feet or more above a lower level, protection is required. Below 4 feet, 1910.28(b)(1) does not require fall protection for an unprotected side or edge (other hazards, e.g., dangerous equipment under (b)(6), can still require protection below 4 feet — see below).

MEASUREMENT CONVENTION

The measurement is the vertical distance from the walking-working surface on which the employee stands to the lower level — not the distance to the edge, and not the height of the employee. "Walking-working surface" is defined in 1910.28/1910.21 as any horizontal or vertical surface on or through which an employee walks, works, or gains access to a work area or workplace location. "Unprotected side or edge" means any side or edge of a walking-working surface (except at entrances and other points of access) where there is no wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system to protect an employee from falling to a lower level.

WHAT SATISFIES THE DUTY AT OR ABOVE 4 FEET

Any one or more of: guardrail system; safety net system; personal fall protection system (personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning system). System criteria and practices are in 29 CFR 1910.29; training in 29 CFR 1910.30.

SCOPE AND CARVE-OUTS A SAFETY ENGINEER SHOULD FLAG

1. Construction is different and is excluded here. Under 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1) the construction trigger is 6 feet. The requester's exclusion of construction is why the answer is 4 feet, not 6 feet. Do not carry the 4-foot figure into Part 1926 work or vice versa.

2. Provisions within 1910.28 that set their own terms (these do not change the general 4-foot trigger; they modify how it applies):
   - Low-slope roofs, 1910.28(b)(13): a distance-from-edge rule, not a height rule. Work less than 6 feet (1.6 m) from the roof edge requires guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or personal fall arrest; the 6-foot and 15-foot figures there are edge-distance bands, not fall-protection trigger heights.
   - Fixed ladders, 1910.28(b)(9): ladders extending more than 24 feet (7.3 m) above a lower level require ladder safety systems or personal fall arrest systems (with the phase-in for cages/wells). The 24-foot figure governs fixed-ladder safety systems; the 4-foot edge trigger still governs unprotected sides and edges of the walking-working surfaces around the ladder.
   - Dangerous equipment, 1910.28(b)(6): protection is required even below 4 feet — employees less than 4 feet above dangerous equipment must be protected by guardrail or travel restraint (unless the equipment is covered or guarded), and at 4 feet or more by guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or personal fall arrest. This is the one place where the trigger effectively goes to zero.
   - Openings, 1910.28(b)(7); hoist areas, (b)(2); holes, (b)(3); ramps, runways and other walkways, (b)(4); stairway landings, (b)(11)(i); rope descent systems, (b)(12)(ii); slaughtering facility platforms, (b)(14)(i): all keyed to 4 feet (1.2 m).
   - Scaffolds, 1910.28(b)(12)(i): fall protection for employees on scaffolds follows 29 CFR Part 1926 Subpart L, even in general industry.

3. Ladders. Portable ladders are governed by 29 CFR 1910.23, not by the 1910.28(b)(1) edge rule; fixed ladders by 1910.23 and 1910.28(b)(9). Do not apply the 4-foot edge trigger to portable ladder use itself.

4. Excluded equipment. 1910.28 does not apply to powered platforms (1910.66(j)), aerial lifts (1910.67(c)(2)(v)), telecommunications work (1910.268(n)(7) and (8)), or electric power generation, transmission, and distribution work (1910.269(g)(2)(i)); those have their own fall-protection provisions.

5. Jurisdictional overlay. About half the states and two territories operate OSHA-approved State Plans. Most adopt the federal 4-foot general-industry trigger, but State Plans may be stricter or have different procedural requirements. For a specific employer, confirm the trigger in the State Plan covering the worksite; the federal figure above is the baseline that applies in federal-jurisdiction states and is the floor most State Plans match.

VERIFICATION

The figure is drawn directly from the current text of 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) as published in the 2025 CFR (govinfo), the current eCFR, and confirmed identically in the 2022 and 2023 CFR editions — i.e., it is the post-2016 walking-working surfaces rule and is stable across editions. The metric equivalent in the regulation is 1.2 m, consistent with 4 ft (1.219 m). Citation for the reader to verify: 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) (and 1910.28(b)(15)).

The first reads: "XVII (7–1–23 Edition) § 1910.28 a lower level is protected from falling"

question: M6
answer:
ANSWER

A helicopter (rotorcraft) beginning a VFR flight in the United States must carry, beyond the fuel needed to fly to the first point of intended landing, reserve fuel sufficient to fly for at least 20 minutes at normal cruising speed. The requirement is 20 minutes for both day and night VFR helicopter operations, and it is the same figure under 14 CFR Part 91 and under 14 CFR Part 135.

1. CONTROLLING REGULATION (Part 91 general aviation)

14 CFR 91.151, 'Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions,' paragraph (b):

  '(b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.'

Three operative elements, which should be read into any flight-planning fuel computation:
  (i) Trip fuel: fuel to the first point of intended landing, computed considering wind and forecast weather conditions.
  (ii) Reserve fuel: 20 minutes of additional flight, computed assuming normal cruising speed (i.e., at the aircraft's normal cruise fuel consumption).
  (iii) The reserve is additive to the trip fuel, not a portion of it, and is measured in flight time, not in gallons.

Note the regulatory term is 'rotorcraft,' so the 20-minute rule covers helicopters and gyroplanes alike.

2. SAME ANSWER UNDER PART 135 (commercial helicopter operators)

14 CFR 135.209(b), 'VFR: Fuel supply':

  '(b) No person may begin a flight operation in a helicopter under VFR unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it has enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.'

FAA Advisory Circular AC 194-1, §5.7.1, restates it: 'Section 135.209(b) states that helicopters must have enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, and to fly after that for at least 20 minutes regardless of day or nighttime.'

Consequence: the answer does not turn on the Part 91 vs. Part 135 question. For VFR helicopters both parts prescribe 20 minutes. (Part 135 operators may still be held to a higher figure by OpSpecs, the operations manual, or company policy — see §6.)

3. DAY VERSUS NIGHT — NO DIFFERENCE FOR HELICOPTERS

91.151(a) and 135.209(a) impose a 30-minute day / 45-minute night reserve on airplanes only. Neither paragraph's day/night escalation reaches rotorcraft/helicopters. A helicopter flying VFR at night still owes 20 minutes, not 45. This is the single most common error in this calculation and should be called out in any training or compliance document derived from this answer.

4. CONVERTING THE 20-MINUTE RESERVE TO A FUEL QUANTITY

The regulation is time-based, so the answer is only convertible to gallons/pounds once the specific helicopter's normal cruising fuel consumption is known. Formula:

  Reserve fuel (gal) = (20 / 60) x normal cruise fuel burn (gal/hr) = normal cruise burn (gal/hr) / 3
  Reserve fuel (lb)  = Reserve fuel (gal) x fuel density (lb/gal)

Use the burn rate for normal cruising speed (the speed/burn the regulation references), not hover, max-range, or best-endurance figures, and not a lower 'loiter' burn chosen to shrink the reserve.

Illustrative conversions only — substitute the actual aircraft's POH/AFM cruise burn and do not treat these as type data:
  - 12 gal/hr cruise -> 12/3 = 4.0 gal reserve
  - 15 gal/hr cruise -> 15/3 = 5.0 gal reserve
  - 30 gal/hr cruise -> 30/3 = 10.0 gal reserve
  - 4.0 gal of avgas at 6.0 lb/gal = 24 lb; 10.0 gal of Jet A at 6.7 lb/gal = 67 lb

Each illustrative figure is exactly burn_rate/3, consistent with the 20-minute requirement; none exceeds or contradicts it.

Total fuel on board at brake release must therefore be at least:

  Trip fuel to first point of intended landing (wind/forecast adjusted)
  + 20 min x normal cruise burn (the reserve)
  + unusable fuel / trapped fuel not available in flight
  + any taxi, run-up, start, and APU/engine-start allowance the operator elects to plan
  + any company/OpSpec adders above the regulatory minimum

Important: the 20 minutes must be burnable in flight. Unusable fuel specified in the POH/AFM does not count toward the reserve. A common practical error is to compute the reserve against total fuel capacity rather than usable fuel.

5. SCOPE LIMITS — WHAT THIS ANSWER DOES NOT COVER

This answer addresses the VFR fuel-reserve minimum only. The following are separate requirements and must not be conflated with it:
  - IFR helicopters: 14 CFR 91.167(a) requires fuel to the first airport of intended landing, plus (unless 91.167(b) is met) fuel to the alternate, plus 30 minutes at normal cruising speed for helicopters (45 minutes for airplanes). Do not apply this 30-minute figure to a VFR flight.
  - IFR alternate planning: 91.169.
  - Preflight action: 91.103 requires the pilot to become familiar with all available information, including fuel requirements, before flight; 91.9 prohibits operating contrary to the AFM/POH limitations.
  - Part 135 operators: 135.209(b) plus any OpSpec, manual, or company fuel policy that is more restrictive. Where a company figure exceeds 20 minutes, the higher figure governs the flight.
  - Non-US operations and ICAO/foreign rules: not authoritative for a US domestic flight; verify separately if the route leaves US airspace, since other states' reserves can be higher.

6. PRACTICAL COMPLIANCE PROCEDURE

Step 1. Confirm the operation is VFR and the aircraft is a rotorcraft/helicopter.
Step 2. Compute trip fuel to the first point of intended landing using forecast winds and temperatures.
Step 3. Take the normal cruise fuel burn from the POH/AFM (or the operator's approved performance data) and divide by 3 to obtain the 20-minute reserve in gallons.
Step 4. Add unusable fuel, start/taxi allowance, and any company or OpSpec adders.
Step 5. Compare the sum against usable fuel on board at brake release; if the sum exceeds usable fuel, the flight cannot legally begin as planned — add a fuel stop or reduce the route.
Step 6. Record the computation (trip fuel, reserve, burn rate source, wind source) in the flight-planning record so the 20-minute reserve is demonstrable on ramp inspection.

7. VERIFICATION NOTE

The 20-minute figure above is taken from the regulatory text quoted in the source passages (91.151(b) and 135.209(b), plus AC 194-1 §5.7.1). Before publication in an operator's manual or training material, re-verify against the current eCFR text of 14 CFR 91.151 and, where applicable, 135.209, since amendments are possible; the quoted 2011 GovInfo text and the current eCFR text agree on the 20-minute rotorcraft reserve.

# Deprecation of TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1

## Direct answers

| Ask | Answer |
|---|---|
| 1. Which RFC deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1? | **RFC 8996**, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1" (K. Moriarty, S. Farrell; March 2021; DOI 10.17487/RFC8996; part of BCP 195). |
| 2. What status did it give the RFCs that had defined them? | **Historic.** RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0) and RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1) were moved to Historic status. |

## Evidence

RFC 8996, Abstract (identical text on rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.html, rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8996/, and the inline-errata rendering):

> "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."

RFC 8996, Section 1 (Introduction):

> "Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1 [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008, which has now itself been superseded by TLS 1.3 [RFC8446]. … Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0. Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to Historic status."

RFC Editor metadata (rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.json) corroborates identity and provenance:

```
doc_id: RFC8996
title: Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1
authors: K. Moriarty; S. Farrell
pub_date: March 2021
pub_status: BEST CURRENT PRACTICE
status: BEST CURRENT PRACTICE
source: Transport Layer Security
obsoletes: RFC5469, RFC7507
updates: RFC3261 … RFC8422 (long list, including RFC7525, RFC6347, RFC2246-adjacent documents)
doi: 10.17487/RFC8996
```

Datatracker document history (datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8996/history/) records publication of RFC 8996 on 2021-03-23, from draft-ietf-tls-oldversions-deprecate-12 (2021-01-21), and later metadata/errata sync events (2023-12-12 BCP195 membership import; 2024-01-17 verified errata tag; 2026-05-20 RFC Editor metadata refresh). None of those events alters the status assignment made in 2021.

## Scope of the status change (exact wording matters)

- **Documents moved to Historic by RFC 8996:** RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0), RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1), RFC 4347 (DTLS 1.0), and RFC 5469 (DES/IDEA cipher suites for TLS).
- **Document obsoleted by RFC 8996:** RFC 7507 (TLS Fallback SCSV), whose functionality TLS 1.3's ServerHello.Random sentinel mechanism supersedes; RFC 8996 states it "has been superseded, and this document marks it as" obsoleted. RFC 5469 is also listed under `obsoletes:` in the RFC Editor metadata in addition to being moved to Historic.
- **Documents updated (not reclassified):** the long `updates:` list, including RFC 7525 (TLS best practices), RFC 6347 (DTLS 1.2 — DTLS 1.0 negotiation now forbidden), and many application-protocol RFCs that normatively referenced TLS 1.0/1.1.

## Terminology note (the trap in this question)

"Deprecated," "obsoleted," and "Historic" are three different things in IETF process, and RFC 8996 uses them distinctly:

1. **Deprecated** is the *protocol-version* verdict: TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0 must no longer be used.
2. **Obsoleted** is a *document* relationship: a newer RFC replaces an older one (RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 were already obsoleted by RFC 5246 in 2008; RFC 5246 in turn by RFC 8446 in 2018). RFC 8996 does *not* obsolete RFC 2246 or RFC 4346 — it does not need to.
3. **Historic** is the *document status* RFC 8996 assigned to RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 (and RFC 4347, RFC 5469). This is the answer to ask 2.

A second trap: RFC 8996's *own* status is **Best Current Practice (BCP 195)**, not Historic. Historic applies to the deprecated protocol-defining documents, not to the deprecating memo. Confusing the two produces a wrong answer to ask 2.

## Verification procedure (reproducible, no tools required)

1. Open `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8996/`; confirm title "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1", status "Best Current Practice", part of BCP 195, March 2021.
2. Read the Abstract; confirm the sentence naming RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 and "moved to Historic status".
3. Open `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc2246/` and `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc4346/`; each status line should read "Historic", with a history entry dated 2021-03-23 attributing the change to RFC 8996.
4. Check `https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.json` for `obsoletes:` / `updates:` to confirm which documents were obsoleted versus merely updated (guards against over-claiming that 8996 obsoletes 2246/4346).
5. Confirm no later RFC has reclassified RFC 2246/4346 back to a standards-track status: the Datatracker history for RFC 8996 shows only metadata, errata, and BCP-195 membership syncs after 2021, and RFC 2246/4346 pages still show Historic. No post-2021 RFC restoring them was found in the fetched sources.

## Residual uncertainty

The grounding supplied consists of RFC Editor and Datatracker pages for RFC 8996 plus two NCSC guidance pages (which independently state: "TLS 1.1 and 1.0 have also been deprecated by the IETF, as outlined in RFC 8996, and should not be used"). The individual status pages for RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 were not fetched by the harness; their Historic status is therefore supported by RFC 8996's own text rather than by a direct reading of those two pages. Step 3 of the procedure above closes that gap in one click and is the only check I could not perform from the supplied passages. This does not block either ask: the deprecating RFC is the authoritative source for the status it assigns.

US Social Security contribution and benefit base (OASDI taxable maximum) for tax year 2026

ANSWER: $184,500

This is the maximum amount of annual earnings subject to the Social Security (OASDI) payroll tax for remuneration paid in calendar year 2026 and for self-employment income earned in tax years beginning in 2026. The same $184,500 figure is the maximum annual earnings counted in computing OASDI benefits.

STATUS: Official, not a projection. Announced by the Social Security Administration in the Federal Register notice 'Cost-of-Living Increase and Other Determinations for 2026,' document 2025-19763, published November 3, 2025 (Federal Register, 90 FR, 2025-19763).

CONTROLLING SOURCES
1. Federal Register, 2025-19763 (Nov. 3, 2025), Determination (1): "The Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI) contribution and benefit base will be $184,500 for remuneration paid in 2026 and self-employment income earned in tax years beginning in 2026." — https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/11/03/2025-19763/cost-of-living-increase-and-other-determinations-for-2026
2. SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, 'Contribution and Benefit Base' table, 2026 = $184,500 — https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html
3. SSA, Fast Facts & Figures About Social Security, 2026: 'Maximum earnings subject to Social Security taxes, 2026: OASDI 184,500; HI No limit.' — https://www.ssa.gov/policy/docs/chartbooks/fast_facts/2026/fast_facts26.html
4. SSA Publication No. 42-007, EFW2 Tax Year 2026 (specifications, 11/12/2026): 'The Social Security Wage Base for tax year 2026 is $184,500'; Social Security tax withheld field 'should not exceed $11,439.00 for tax year 2026.' — https://www.ssa.gov/employer/efw/26efw2.pdf

HOW THE FIGURE IS DERIVED (Social Security Act sec. 230(b), as recited in the notice)
- The 2026 base is the larger of (1) the 1994 base of $60,600 multiplied by the ratio of the national average wage index for 2024 to that for 1992, or (2) the current (2025) base of $176,100; the result is rounded to the nearest multiple of $300.
- Computation: $60,600 × ($69,846.57 / $22,935.42) = $184,548.71 → rounded to $184,500.
- Because $184,500 exceeds $176,100, the 2026 OASDI contribution and benefit base is $184,500.
- Arithmetic checks: $184,500 is an exact multiple of $300 (615 × 300); $184,548.71 is $48.71 above $184,500 and $251.29 below $184,800, so $184,500 is the correct nearest multiple.

ASSOCIATED AMOUNTS (for the requester's convenience; these are not the base itself)
- OASDI tax rate, 2026: 6.2% each for employee and employer (12.4% for self-employment income).
- Maximum annual OASDI tax at the base, 2026: employee $11,439.00 (= $184,500 × 6.2%); employer $11,439.00; self-employed $22,878.00 (= $184,500 × 12.4%). The $11,439.00 figure matches the cap stated in SSA EFW2 Pub. 42-007 for tax year 2026.
- Medicare (HI): no earnings cap in 2026 — the OASDI base does not apply to HI.

SCOPE NOTES / FIGURES NOT TO CONFUSE WITH THE ANSWER
- Year: the answer is 2026. SSA's page also shows $192,300 for 2027; that is a different year and is not the answer. The 2025 base was $176,100.
- Old-law contribution and benefit base, 2026: $137,100. This is a separate statutory figure used by the Railroad Retirement program (tier II tax liabilities and benefits), PBGC for ERISA maximum guarantee determinations, and SSA for special-minimum-benefit years of coverage and for certain pension offsets. It is NOT the payroll-tax base.
- OASDI retirement earnings test monthly exempt amounts, 2026: $2,040 (beneficiaries attaining NRA after 2026) and $5,430 (those attaining NRA in 2026). These limit benefits paid to working beneficiaries; they are not a tax base.
- Quarter of coverage, 2026: $1,890 of earnings per credit (max four credits, $7,560).
- PIA formula bend points, 2026: $1,286 and $7,749. Maximum family benefit bend points, 2026: $1,643, $2,371, $3,093.
- 2026 COLA: 2.8%.

ONE-LINE CITATION FORM: Social Security Administration, 'Cost-of-Living Increase and Other Determinations for 2026,' 2025-19763, Fed. Reg. (Nov. 3, 2025), Determination (1); see also SSA, Contribution and Benefit Base, https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html — OASDI contribution and benefit base for 2026: $184,500.

ANSWER

The 2026 limit on an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan, before any catch-up contribution, is $24,500.

This is the IRC §402(g)(1) limitation on the exclusion for elective deferrals. It is also expressed as the lesser of $24,500 or 100% of the employee's compensation for the year.

AUTHORITY

- IRS Notice 2025-67 (2026 cost-of-living adjustments), published in Internal Revenue Bulletin 2025-49, page 761: "The limitation under section 402(g)(1) on the exclusion for elective deferrals described in section 402(g)(3), which includes elective deferrals made to the Thrift Savings Plan, is increased from $23,500 to $24,500."
- IRS, COLA increases for dollar limitations on benefits and contributions, 2026 column for "401(k), 403(b), profit-sharing plans, etc. — Elective deferrals": $24,500 (2025: $23,500; 2024: $23,000; 2023: $22,500).
- IRS, Retirement topics — 401(k) and profit-sharing plan contribution limits: "The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments."
- IRS, Retirement topics — Contributions: "The basic limit on elective deferrals is $24,500 in 2026 ... or 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less."

WHAT THE $24,500 DOES AND DOES NOT INCLUDE

- Includes: pre-tax (traditional) elective deferrals and Roth elective deferrals. Pre-tax and Roth employee elective deferrals share this single combined §402(g) limit; electing Roth does not create an additional allowance.
- Excludes: age-50+ catch-up contributions under §414(v). For 2026 the separate catch-up limits are $8,000 (participants age 50 or over) and $11,250 (participants who attain age 60, 61, 62, or 63 in 2026). These are added on top of the $24,500 and are not part of the base limit.
